title: What changed
dek: Most family archives publish only what they found. This one publishes what it looked for, what it found, what it did not find, and what it had to take back.
lead: This page is the archive's working record. Each entry is one research pass: the sources opened, what came out of them, and which pages of this site changed as a result. Where a pass produced an error that was later corrected, it says so and links to the correction rather than quietly editing the history.

days.title: A living person is now a name, a town and a country, where before there was nothing
did: THE RULE CHANGED, AND IT CHANGED IN THE DATA. Until today this archive published no living person as a person: no page, no dates, no birthplace, and no name where it would stand as somebody's spouse, parent or child. David ruled, with the tree's 2,034 living people in front of him, that it adopts the standard the Defranceschi archive keeps: a living person is named, with their town and country, and nothing more. tools/build_site_data.py now BUILDS a living person out of a name, their relationships and the town and country of their birthplace, and never reads the rest of their record, so there is no date for a page to forget to hide.

A RECORDED DEATH IS A DEATH. The upper-bound test still decides who is living, with one exception that David ruled the same day: a person the tree RECORDS as deceased, by a death or burial entry with or without a date, is dead. Before, the build ignored a death entry that carried no date, so 544 of the tree's 2,034 living were people the tree itself said had died; the tree now judges 1,490 living. Those people are ordinary dead people: no «treated as living» on their pages, indexable, and showing only what the tree already held for them. 17 of the 85 first named moved from living to dead on that rule.

TWO KINDS OF LIVING PERSON ARE LEFT OUT ALTOGETHER, also David's ruling of that day. The living woman whose DNA result /dna/ describes is held out by id, so that page's sentence that she is not named stays true; and every living person with no birth year in the tree who has a living parent is held out by rule, because with no year nobody can tell a child from an adult. Neither has a page, a record, or a name as anybody's relative; they are not in any committed data file or tsv either. The rule is gedcom.held_out(); tools/check_living.py recomputes it separately from the tree and searches for their names, tools/check_living_standard.py proves their ids are absent without a tree. Six were met in this build and left out; the rule catches 377 anywhere in the tree besides the one held by id.

THE GATES WERE TURNED THE OTHER WAY. check_living.py used to search every page for 1,768 living name phrases and refuse to ship if one appeared. A name is allowed now, so it searches instead for everything else the tree holds about a living person (every full date, note, source, occupation and long place) in the built site and in every file the repository tracks, and checks that the data and the tree agree about who is living. A new gate, check_living_standard.py, needs only the committed data and the built pages, so it runs in the deploy: every living page is noindex, carries no structured data, no table, no image and no year; none is in the sitemap, the search index or whoindex.json; and a dead person's page must behave the opposite way, or the build is not clean. Both were shown to fail on planted faults.
found: 35 living people now have a page, each noindex; 27 more are named without one, as a spouse, brother, sister or parent. The tree judges 1,490 living; the archive gives a page only to the numbered ancestors and the thirteen families
the search index and whoindex.json hold no living person, and no living name is left in the text of the pages the search indexes
17 people first named as living are now dead on the strength of the tree's own death or burial entry; 6 living people are held out altogether (1 by id, 5 by rule)
the six people named on purpose in prose, and the confirmation recorded for each; none of them was downgraded
every address of a person who has died: the living are slugged after the dead, so admitting them moved no published URL

days.title: The archive moves to darcy.defranceski.com, and loses two and a half hours of its own readership on the way
found: the archive is now at darcy.defranceski.com. The old address redirects, with the path kept, so nothing anybody has linked or bookmarked breaks
2h 39m of readership figures, 09:14 to 11:53 UTC, logged into another family's GoatCounter account and not recoverable
the canonical on all 858 pages, which the same fault had pointed at a different archive — caught in a scratch build and never published
robots.txt, which went on naming a sitemap at the old origin while everything else had moved
two gates — one on whose counter the built pages name, one on the three files that state this archive's address
0 pages without an inbound link, 0 broken asset references, 0 of this archive's own citations dead
did: WHY THE ADDRESS CHANGED AT ALL. defranceski.com is a GitHub Pages site served by its own repository, and project sites do not inherit it — defranceski.com/TheDArcy/ returns 404. So a subdomain was the only clean route rather than a preference, and six sister archives are moving the same way.

THE READERSHIP GAP, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH READING. Every page this archive served between 09:14 and 11:53 UTC on 12 October reported its pageview to thedefranceski.goatcounter.com — the Defranceschi family's account — instead of its own. That is about two and a half hours of visits at both addresses, and they cannot be separated out of the other account afterwards. So this archive's figures have a hole in them on that afternoon, and the hole is not a quiet period. Anyone reading the counter should know the number is short by whatever those hours held.

HOW A DOMAIN MOVE REACHES A COUNTER. The layout asked which of the seven archives it was building by matching `base`, which is "/TheDArcy" for a project site and the EMPTY STRING once an archive has its own domain. Five archives had moved, so five shared that key, and the lookup returned the first of them. Name, accent and counter code are all read off that one answer. The data was never wrong — this archive's entry has always said its counter is `thedarcy`, and editing it would have broken the only part that was correct. The lookup is now matched by ORIGIN.

THE SAME FAULT HAD ALREADY BEEN CAUGHT ONCE, WHICH IS WHY THE SECOND ONE STINGS. It first appeared as a canonical — every page of this archive declaring archive.defranceski.com as its true address, which is the one SEO error that hands your pages to somebody else. That was found in a scratch build and the move was held, unpublished, until the shared kit was fixed. The counter was the same collision reaching a different line, and it went out.

AND THE VERIFICATION THAT MISSED IT WAS NOT CARELESS, IT WAS NARROW. The held build was checked on canonical, og:url, og:site_name and theme-color. Four fields, all correct — and all four written by one component, which the kit had already repaired. The counter is written by a different line of a layout that does not go through it. A verification is only as wide as the number of INDEPENDENT SOURCES it touches, not the number of fields it lists, and this one reported a single source wearing four hats as four confirmations. It is own error 57.

SO THE NEW GATE READS THE BUILT PAGE AND NOTHING ELSE. `tools/check_counter.py` opens every page of the finished site and refuses if any of them names a counter that is not this archive's. It finds the archive by origin, because matching by base is the bug it exists to catch, and it was pointed at the broken build FIRST and seen to refuse 856 pages before it was trusted — a gate that has only ever been watched to pass is being trusted on its intentions. The sharpest version of that rule came from a sister archive the same afternoon: its own check re-derived the counter using the very rule that was broken, so it confirmed the fault instead of finding it, and would have gone on reporting it after the fix. A check that models the code instead of reading its output can only ever agree with it.

A SECOND GATE, for the thing that nearly went unnoticed underneath all this: robots.txt was still sending crawlers to a sitemap at the old address, on a green build, because no gate read it. Three files state where this archive lives — the site config, the CNAME that keeps the domain attached, and robots.txt — and `siteOrigin` now refuses a build in which they disagree. All three of its failure modes were provoked and watched to refuse before it was believed.

WHAT THE MOVE DID NOT BREAK. Every internal link, the redirect from the old /what-we-got-wrong address, the sitemap, the search index and all 858 pages came through intact, and the old address redirects with the path preserved rather than dumping anybody at the front page. Four letters in the working notes still quote the old address and have deliberately NOT been rewritten: whether they were posted is not recorded here, and a sent letter is a record of what was sent.

days.title: The whole site read against itself, and eleven findings turned out never to have reached a page
found: two recorded relationships that had never drawn: John Atwell and Richard Atkinson were each AMBIGUOUS in the tree, and the edges now carry the year that settles them
four relationships added this week were REFUSED by the chart and the refusal was right — the second party in each exists only in a document, and a record line is not an edge
the Moreton Bay Courier of 23 December 1854 was read for the General Hewitt and DOES NOT CARRY HER — the arrival date rests on the register alone, and now says so
the first Military Medal has no citation anywhere: the Gazette promulgates the award and never says what it was for
a wall that is not money — the will of a Chepstow mariner, digitised at the National Library of Wales behind a bot check this archive will not pass
FreeREG offers County Limerick and holds NOTHING behind it, so every free Limerick search was searching a county that is not in the index
two record classes that cannot be searched by name at all — feet of fines catalogued at piece level, and the Gloucestershire editions in copyright
the coverage verdicts and the Trove gazette key, both of them faults in this archive's own instruments, now published on the page whose numbers they affected
the snapshot coverage figure is computed by the tool and read by the page, after a sentence saying 70 of 84 survived a week into the instrument saying 73 of 87
0 pages with no inbound link, 0 broken asset references, and 0 of this archive's own citations dead — the nine candidates are all inherited from the GEDCOM export
did: DAVID ASKED FOR THE WHOLE SITE TO BE READ — people pages, visuals, trees, writeups, snapshots and links — AND THE GATES ALL SAID OK BEFORE ANY OF THIS WAS FOUND. That is the useful part. Every gate passed on the first run of the audit, and eleven findings were still sitting in the data without ever reaching the page they belong to. A green build means no rule was broken; it does not mean the archive says what it knows.

THE FIRST THING CHECKED WAS THE WRONG THING, AND IT COST AN HOUR. Four relationships documented this week looked absent from the charts, so they were added to the edge list and the result was verified against `register.json`'s `linked` — which is a COUNT OF ENTRIES CARRYING A LINK and has nothing whatever to do with relationships. The edges live in `provenance.json`. The tool had reported its own failure plainly, in its own output, and it was not read: NINE REL NAMES THAT DREW NO EDGE, printed as a bare list for weeks.

AND THE REFUSALS WERE RIGHT. Of the nine, two were ambiguous names — two John Atwells, three Richard Atkinsons — and the tree settled both by its own id links: James Atwell's parents are John Atwell and Maria Rossiter, and John Atwell born 1824 lists that same James by identifier as his child. Those two now draw, with the Queensland death registration as the reason. The other seven cannot ever draw, because the person at the far end exists only in a document and a chart draws the tree. FOUR OF THEM WERE THIS SESSION'S OWN, ADDED ON A WRONG DIAGNOSIS, AND THEY ARE GONE AGAIN.

A LIST OF NAMES IS NOT A DIAGNOSIS, so the reporter now says WHY each name fails — ambiguous, document-only, or absent — because the three want three different answers and a bare list invites none of them.

ELEVEN ROWS CLAIMED A PAGE THAT HAD NEVER CARRIED THEM. The `published` gate counts these and had been printing «11 quiet» without anyone acting on it. They were not noise. The Moreton Bay Courier had been read for the General Hewitt and had NOT confirmed the arrival — an honest negative result that no reader could see. The London Gazette had been checked for Vivian Sneyd's first Military Medal and gazettes it without a citation. The National Library of Wales serves a bot check over a digitised will, and `/behind-the-paywall` — the page about walls — did not mention the one wall that is not money. FreeREG offers County Limerick with no data behind it, and `/atkinson` did not say so. All eleven now reach their page, and the count is 0.

TWO OF THEM WERE FILED ON A PAGE THAT RENDERS A DIFFERENT FILE. `/coverage` renders `indexes.json`; `coverage.json` renders on `/searched`. Two findings about Gloucestershire record classes pointed at `/coverage` and could never have appeared there whatever was written. They are re-filed on `/swonhungre`, where the surname they are about lives.

AND ONE WARNING WAS THE INSTRUMENT, NOT THE ARCHIVE. The errand for the will of THOMAS SANNIGER, Able Seaman of HMS Eurydice, was graded on the single word «Seamen» — taken from «Seamen's wills are short» — and reported as unpublished on a page that names SANNIGER three times. The test asks the finding first, which is right, and then refused to look at the identification beside it, which is not. ONE COMMON WORD IS NOT A DISTINCTIVE TOKEN: below two tokens it now reads both fields. Same fault as the version that certified a row because a page said «Wales», pointing the other way.

A FIGURE IN PROSE GOES STALE THE NEXT TIME THE TOOL RUNS. The snapshot count was written into a sentence as «70 of 84» and the instrument now says 73 of 87 — one week. `snapshot.py` writes the number where the page can read it, and `/sources` carries it with the hosts that decline to be archived named, so the page cannot disagree with the tool. The dated changelog entries are left as they were: they were true on the day and rewriting them would falsify the record.

WHAT THE AUDIT DID NOT FIND IS WORTH SAYING. No page is without an inbound link; no asset reference is broken; no citation this archive chose for itself is dead, and the nine dead ones are all somebody else's footnotes inherited from the GEDCOM export. 858 pages built, every gate green, 248 record lines reaching 62 of 62 people in the tree.

days.title: The Sanigars, Sneyds and Wakefields get the same treatment, and Oswestry hands over a family
found: David Oliver, COOPER of Cross Street, Oswestry — buried 1808 aged 59, with three children baptised
Elizabeth Margaret Oliver has siblings for the first time: Dianna 1777 and David 1789
Jabez Wakefield was EX-MAYOR OF ROCKHAMPTON; Hiram was a Brisbane timber merchant and J.P. for twenty years
the Sneyd marriage is not in the printed Oswestry register — which stops in 1808, one year short
the printed Madeley register located — William Sneyd the WEAVER is in it, and Madeley turns out to be two townships
/abbas-kooli — a page of his own for the governor, linked from his father
tools/snapshot.py — does a PERMANENT COPY exist of every source this archive cites? 47 of 83 did
a candidate marriage for the Oswestry Olivers — David Oliver and MARY OWENS, Llanyblodwel 1772, graded as a candidate
permanent copies — 15 of 83 at the start, 70 of 84 now, and the 14 left are hosts that refuse to be archived
Robert D'Arcy was Commanding Engineer at Copenhagen in 1807, under the future Duke of Wellington
Elizabeth Eleanor D'Arcy — Allen's Indian Mail carried her marriage, and that is NOT evidence about her parentage
Joseph D'Arcy in Persia, from an eyewitness — he sailed with the embassy, was sent to draw ruins, and commanded an attack
Porter vol. II re-scanned with the corrected pattern — genuinely no D'Arcy in it
/joseph-darcy — the Persian service from the Ambassador's brother: he was the embassy's ARTIST, and six plates of a scholarly work are his
«Abbas Mirza is this archive's identification, not the Calendar's» — answered, by a man who was there
did: DAVID ASKED FOR THE OTHER THREE LINES AND OSWESTRY ANSWERED FIRST. The Shropshire Parish Registers for the DIOCESE OF ST ASAPH are printed, free and out of copyright, and eight volumes were downloaded whole and read. They give DAVID OLIVER, COOPER, OF CROSS STREET, OSWESTRY — an occupation and an address this archive did not have — BURIED AT OSWESTRY ON 21 JUNE 1808, AGED 59, which puts his birth about 1749. With Mary he baptises DIANNA on 23 MARCH 1777, ELIZABETH on 19 MAY 1782 and DAVID on 12 JULY 1789. Elizabeth is this archive's Elizabeth Margaret Oliver, who married Samuel Sneyd, and THESE ARE THE FIRST SIBLINGS SHE HAS EVER HAD HERE.

AND A ONE-DIGIT DISAGREEMENT THAT NOBODY CAN SETTLE FROM HERE. The printed transcript reads «Elizabeth, d. of David Oliver, Cross St., & Mary, B. 7»; FindMyPast's index of the same register line says she was BORN 17 MAY. Two transcriptions of one entry, agreeing on the baptism date, the parents and the year, and differing by a single digit on the day of birth. NEITHER IS THE REGISTER. It is recorded as a disagreement rather than resolved by preferring whichever source was read second.

THE SNEYD MARRIAGE IS NOT IN THE PRINTED OSWESTRY REGISTER AND THAT PROVES NOTHING, WHICH IS THE WHOLE POINT. The eight volumes print 581 Oswestry marriages and the only Sneyds anywhere in them are the GENTRY SNEYDS OF BISHTON — the same Staffordshire family the tree once tried to graft this line onto. BUT THE PRINTED MARRIAGE RUN ENDS IN 1808, and Samuel Sneyd's marriage to Elizabeth Oliver is placed about 1809. THE TRANSCRIPT STOPS ONE YEAR SHORT OF THE QUESTION. An hour was nearly spent reporting an absence that covers everything except the year that matters.

THE WAKEFIELDS TURN OUT TO HAVE BEEN PUBLIC MEN. JABEZ WAKEFIELD stands in the obituary list of Slater's Queensland Almanac for 1904, under the 7th of February, as «AN OLD RESIDENT AND EX-MAYOR OF ROCKHAMPTON» — this archive already held his death as 8 February 1903 from the Queensland register, so the two agree to a day, and WHAT IS NEW IS THAT HE HAD BEEN MAYOR. HIRAM WAKEFIELD is a Brisbane figure across twenty years: the Aldine History of Queensland of 1888 twice describes men who «entered the employ of HIRAM WAKEFIELD, TIMBER MERCHANT»; in 1868 Slater's has him running a TWO-HORSE COACH between Brisbane and Sandgate; and from 1882 to 1891 he is a trustee and then a director, «Hiram Wakefield, Esq., J.P.», beside Hon. James Swan M.L.C. and JAMES R. DICKSON, LATER PREMIER OF QUEENSLAND.

ONE READING WAS REFUSED. The 1888 almanac prints him «M.L.A.» where the volumes for 1882, 1883, 1884, 1885, 1886, 1887, 1890 and 1891 all print «J.P.». ONE AGAINST EIGHT IS A COMPOSITOR'S SLIP AND NOT A SEAT IN THE LEGISLATIVE ASSEMBLY, and it goes down as a discrepancy. THE SANIGARS GAVE NOTHING: «Hannah Saniger» returns four hits and all four are four scans of one Toronto history naming a different Hannah Saniger who married a George Dale. Written down because the name is rare enough that the next person will find it too.

AND THE SNEYD ORIGIN HAS A PRINTED REGISTER AFTER ALL, THOUGH IT WILL NOT OPEN. The Staffordshire Parish Register Society printed MADELEY, and the volume is on the Internet Archive — LENDING-RESTRICTED, text returning HTTP 401, a borrow needing an account this archive will not make. ITS PUBLIC SNIPPETS STILL GAVE SOMETHING: «13 MARGARET D. OF WILLIAM SNEYD, WEAVER» and «THOMAS S. OF WILLIAM SNEYD OF GT. MADELEY». THE WORD «WEAVER» IS THE MATCH — this archive holds Samuel Sneyd baptised at Madeley All Saints on 4 June 1781, father WILLIAM SNEYD, WEAVER. WHAT IT DOES NOT ESTABLISH IS ANY RELATIONSHIP: the snippets carry NO YEARS, so a Margaret and a Thomas are children of a weaver of that name in that parish and nothing more until somebody reads the book.

AND IT SETTLED ONE THING FOR NOTHING. THE REGISTER DISTINGUISHES «GT. MADELEY» FROM «L. MADELEY» — GREAT AND LITTLE MADELEY, two townships. This archive has written «Madeley All Saints» on the Sneyd origin from the beginning and HAS NEVER ASKED WHICH HALF THE FAMILY LIVED IN. It is the same shape as the two Ingouvilles that cost a day this week and the two Kingswoods that nearly cost the Sanigars their county — CAUGHT THIS TIME BEFORE IT COST ANYTHING, which is the first time that has happened.

AND THE RESEARCH GOT A PAGE INSTEAD OF A REGISTER LINE. George Abbas Kooli D'Arcy had been going into this archive the way everything does — record lines in the register, rows on the search log, a paragraph in the changes — and that is right for a baptism and wrong for a life. HE NOW HAS A DOSSIER AT /ABBAS-KOOLI: the corrected name of 1837, the adjutancy, the captaincy printed twice, Bombay, the West India Regiment, the Gambia from 1859, Baddiboo and Sabba and Tubabecolong, the sword of honour, the Falklands from 1870, and the death in Devon. It is linked from his father's page, so the published gate counts it rather than calling it an orphan, and it carries the two things a page like this should carry: WHAT IS STILL NOT KNOWN (whether he ever married) and HOW HE WAS FOUND, which is the transferable part.

AND A NEW QUESTION THIS ARCHIVE HAD NEVER ASKED. check_cites.py asks whether a citation STILL RESOLVES TODAY. IT DOES NOT ASK WHETHER THE READER COULD STILL SEE WHAT THIS ARCHIVE SAW IF IT STOPPED. tools/snapshot.py asks that: for every citation this archive CHOSE — the GEDCOM's myheritage links are somebody else's footnotes — does a capture exist in the Wayback Machine? THE FIRST ANSWER WAS 15 OF 83. A footnote to a page that has gone is a footnote to nothing, and the reader cannot tell it apart from a good one.

THE FIRST VERSION OF THAT TOOL WAS WRONG IN A FAMILIAR WAY AND WAS CAUGHT BY RUNNING IT. It asked the Wayback Machine to capture twelve archive.org URLs AND GOT TWELVE 523s BACK — the Internet Archive quite properly declining to snapshot itself. A CITATION TO THE INTERNET ARCHIVE IS ALREADY A PERMANENT COPY, and counting those as unprotected both flattered the problem and would have sent the next person chasing a capture that cannot exist. With that fixed the honest figure was 46 OF 83, twenty-three of them permanent because they ARE the archive. Captures have since been requested for the rest, twenty at a time with a pause between, because a request to a public archive to crawl a public page should look like a request and not a flood.

AND THE OSWESTRY VOLUMES WERE ALREADY ON DISK, SO ONE MORE QUESTION COST NOTHING. The baptisms give Elizabeth Margaret Oliver's mother only as «Mary». The printed LLANYBLODWEL register has «1772, JUNE 12. DAVID OLIVER OF OSWESTRY P: BAC: & MARY OWENS SP: … lic: mar». WHAT FITS: he is of Oswestry parish, where the baptisms are; the forename pair matches; 1772 sits properly before Dianna in 1777, Elizabeth in 1782 and David in 1789; and a David Oliver, cooper, buried at Oswestry in 1808 aged 59 was about twenty-three in 1772. WHAT DOES NOT: NOTHING LINKS THE ENTRY TO THE BAPTISMS EXCEPT THOSE FITS, and David and Mary are two of the commonest names on this border — the same eight volumes hold David Olivers at Blodwell, Trefyrclawdd, Pentreshanel, Sweeney and Willow Street across a century.

THE CONTROL IS THAT THE SHORTLIST IS ONE LONG. All eight volumes were searched for EVERY marriage of a David Oliver: between 1765 and 1782 there is EXACTLY ONE, and the only other in the series is «1799, May 10. David Oliver, bac: & Anne Morris, sp:» — wrong wife, wrong decade. IF IT IS THE RIGHT MARRIAGE, ELIZABETH MARGARET OLIVER'S MOTHER WAS MARY OWENS and the Sneyd line gains a surname it has never had. IT IS NOT YET THE RIGHT MARRIAGE, and the register line says so in those words rather than quietly promoting a good fit into a fact.

AND THE SNAPSHOT COUNT FINISHED AT 70 OF 84, FROM 15. The captures were requested twenty at a time with a pause between, because asking a public archive to crawl a public page should look like a request and not a flood. THE FOURTEEN THAT REMAIN ARE NOT A JOB UNDONE AND THE TOOL NOW SAYS SO IN ITS OWN VOICE. Every one of them resolves perfectly and simply declines to be archived: NLA.GOV.AU SIX TIMES — Trove's article permalinks — FINDAGRAVE THREE TIMES, FamilySearch's tree, the Anubis-gated Seine-Maritime viewer, FIBIS, and two dynamic download endpoints. A HOST THAT DECLINES TO BE ARCHIVED IS A FACT ABOUT THE HOST, and a bare number would have read as work nobody had got round to, so the tool prints them grouped by host with that sentence attached.

AND PORTER'S THIRD CAMPAIGN TURNED OUT TO BE THE BEST OF THEM. The index gave «Copenhagen, 243» and the first full-text pass had found nothing there, so it was written down as THE INDEX'S CLAIM rather than a passage read. It is a passage, and it reads: the force sailed from Yarmouth Roads on 27 July 1807 with 20,000 men «under the command of MAJOR-GENERAL SIR ARTHUR WELLESLEY», and «THE ENGINEERS CONSISTED OF LIEUTENANT-COLONEL R. D'ARCY, COMMANDING ENGINEER; Captains R. Fletcher, J. F. Birch and S. R. Chapman; Second Captains C. W. PASLEY, H. Goldfinch and C. S. Rhodes; First Lieutenant G. Collyer.» TWO OF THE MEN UNDER HIM BECAME FAMOUS — Richard Fletcher, Wellington's chief engineer in the Peninsula, killed at San Sebastian; and Charles Pasley, who founded the school of military engineering AT CHATHAM, WHERE D'ARCY HIMSELF DIED AS COMMANDANT TWENTY YEARS LATER.

AND THE BOOK'S OWN INDEX IS WHAT FOUND IT, WHICH IS THE LESSON. The first pass matched SEVEN instances of the surname and MISSED THIS ONE, because the scanner had set it «D‘Arcy» with a LEFT single quotation mark where every other instance in the volume uses a right one. THE SEARCH WAS WRONG AND THE INDEX WAS RIGHT. Nobody would have gone looking for page 243 if Porter had not listed it. AN INDEX IS A CONTROL ON A FULL-TEXT SEARCH — an independent statement of what the book contains, made by somebody who could read it — and after a week of full-text searching this archive now has a reason to read the index first.

AND A TEMPTING INFERENCE WAS REFUSED. ALLEN'S INDIAN MAIL CARRIED THE RUCK MARRIAGE: «Groom RUCK, Arthur Ashley · Bride D'ARCY, ELIZABETH ELEANOR · 1877» — a second, independent record of the Penzance marriage, reported from the India side. IT IS NOT EVIDENCE THAT SHE WAS ONE OF THE INDIAN D'ARCYS, and it would have been very easy to say that it was. Arthur Ashley Ruck was himself an India-serving officer in the Afghan war of 1878-81, so the Anglo-Indian paper had every reason to print his marriage whoever he married. FIBIS holds NO BAPTISM for her across two million names. Whose daughter she was is exactly as open as it was yesterday.

AND THE PERSIAN SERVICE STOPPED BEING A SENTENCE IN AN OBITUARY. This archive has had Joseph D'Arcy's five years in Persia only from his own death notice of 1848, looking back forty years. JAMES MORIER WAS SECRETARY OF THE BRITISH EMBASSY AND SAILED WITH HIM, and his book names him three times. The voyage out: «On board the CHICHESTER STORE-SHIP, which accompanied us, were MAJOR (NOW COLONEL) D'ARCY, and MAJOR STONE, OF THE ARTILLERY, WHO DIED IN PERSIA; and TEN PRIVATES OF THE ARTILLERY.» And then, when Sir Gore Ouseley scattered his suite across Persia to record antiquities — Sir William Ouseley to Fasa for the tomb of Cyrus, the Hon. Mr Gordon to Shouster for ancient Susa, Morier himself to Persepolis — «COLONEL D'ARCY PROCEEDED TO FIROUZABAD, WHERE WE HAD HEARD OF SOME REMARKABLE SCULPTURES.» An artillery officer sent to draw rock reliefs, which is not how this archive had pictured him.

AND HE COMMANDED AN ATTACK, WHICH IS THE ONLY ACTION OF HIS THIS ARCHIVE HAS. Abbas Mirza marched on Mogan; eight hundred Russians with two guns held the village of SULTANBOOT. «THE ATTACK, UNDER THE COMMAND OF COLONEL D'ARCY, TOOK PLACE IN THE MORNING. The Russians, in negligent confidence, were surprised to see A WELL-DIRECTED FIRE OF GRAPE open upon them, WHICH IN A SHORT TIME KILLED 300 OF THEIR MEN… they capitulated. ONE OF THE ARTICLES OF CAPITULATION WAS, THAT THEIR HEADS WERE NOT TO BE CUT OFF.» The Persians first reported two thousand killed and five thousand taken, and told Morier to his face that they had inflated it because «THIS IS THE FIRST TIME OUR TROOPS HAVE MADE ANY STAND AT ALL AGAINST THE RUSSIANS». NO YEAR IS PUT ON IT HERE: the passage carries none, thirty thousand characters before it hold no date, and the book spans 1810 to 1816.

AND THE INDEX FOUND HIM, FOR THE SECOND TIME IN ONE DAY. A full-text search of Morier matched ONE instance of the surname — THE INDEX ENTRY, «D'Arcy, Colonel, 2. 68. 186». All three body passages were missed because the book sets his name in LOWER CASE, «d'Arcy», and the pattern demanded a capital D. Earlier the same day Porter's Copenhagen page was missed over a LEFT rather than a right quotation mark. TWO DIFFERENT CHARACTERS, TWO MISSED PAGES, AND THE INDEX RIGHT BOTH TIMES. Porter's volume II was re-scanned with the corrected pattern in case it had hidden anything: it had not, and its nothing is now a measured nothing.

AND THE PERSIAN SERVICE TURNED OUT TO BE A WHOLE LIFE. SIR WILLIAM OUSELEY WAS THE AMBASSADOR'S BROTHER AND SHARED A HOUSE WITH HIM AT TABRIZ, and his three volumes name Joseph D'Arcy thirty-four times. HE WAS THE EMBASSY'S ARTIST. Ouseley's preface: «THE PLATES WHICH CONTRIBUTE MOST HIGHLY TO THE EMBELLISHMENT OF THIS VOLUME have been engraved from drawings made by MY ACCOMPLISHED AND AMIABLE FRIEND… Those plates are numbered II. IV. V. XI. XVIII, and XX.» They are signed «Colonel D'Arcy del.» and they are the cave temples at ELEPHANTA, the great Sasanian sculpture at SHAPUR, a nautch dance, a well near Bushehr with mount Halilah behind it, and the Ambassador's house at Rio. At the tomb called Solomon's Mother's grave Ouseley sketched the same view and then PREFERRED D'ARCY'S TO HIS OWN. He also helped take squeezes of a Pahlavi inscription, «impressing every form of the letters on paper slightly wetted for the purpose, and applied to the very stone»; and at Isfahan he drew the poet KAZEM WALEH, eighty years old and composing his own epitaph, who refused until flattered, tried on every turban he owned, and then «SAT MOST COMPLACENTLY WHILE COLONEL D'ARCY FINISHED AN ADMIRABLE LIKENESS».

AND IT ANSWERED A QUESTION THIS PAGE HAD WRITTEN DOWN AND LEFT OPEN. The Joseph D'Arcy page said, of the Persian service: «WHAT IS STILL MISSING IS THE YEARS HE WAS THERE AND THE NAME OF THE PRINCE HE SERVED — ABBAS MIRZA IS THIS ARCHIVE'S IDENTIFICATION, NOT THE CALENDAR'S.» Ouseley names the prince outright and dates the moment. NOVEMBER 1811, AT TEHRAN: the Prince asked for British officers, «but THE KING WOULD NOT CONSENT that any of those officers should leave Tehran WITHOUT KHELAATS, OR DRESSES OF HONOUR»; they were given them and «PROCEEDED TO JOIN THE ARMY OF ABBAS MIRZA, THE PRINCE ROYAL, AT TABRIZ». By June 1812 he was «MY FRIEND MAJOR D'ARCY, WHO, AS SENIOR OFFICER, COMMANDED IN THE MILITARY DEPARTMENT» — two Russian envoys and a French officer lodged in his house, and Ouseley left for Constantinople from it on 1 July 1812. THE ARCHIVE'S GUESS IS NOW THE AMBASSADOR'S BROTHER'S STATEMENT.

ONE DATE IS LEFT DISAGREEING AND ONE MISTAKE OF MY OWN IS WORTH RECORDING. A footnote in Ouseley's first volume dates the Firuzabad excursion to «THE SUMMER OF 1814», but the narrative places that dispersal in 1811 and Ouseley left Persia in July 1812; either the year is a slip for 1811 or it records a later visit, AND THIS ARCHIVE DOES NOT PICK ONE. And in writing the new section I OVERWROTE THE PAGE'S EXISTING «persia» BLOCK, because the key was already taken and I did not look. The PAGES gate caught it within the minute — the old block renders plain and my markdown came through raw — and the original is restored, with the new material under its own key beside it. A GATE THAT CATCHES YOU CLOBBERING YOUR OWN PAGE IS WORTH THE TROUBLE OF HAVING WRITTEN IT.

days.title: A novelist published this family's photographs in 1972 and nobody here had asked who she was

Annie Adams's middle name settled at HEWISH by three records that did not copy each other

George Abbas Kooli D'Arcy governed the Falkland Islands 1870-1876 as well as the Gambia
the Army Lists of 1775-1783 — Robert and Constantine are in them, the colonel who was to prove the descent is not

did: THE WORK LIST WAS EMPTY OF ANYTHING THIS ARCHIVE COULD START, SO IT WENT LOOKING. The Internet Archive's full text was searched for «ABBAS KOOLI» — a name chosen because nothing else in print shares it — and returned 329 hits. THE FIRST IS A BOOK ABOUT THIS FAMILY. Ancestral Voices, by the novelist BERTA RUCK (1878-1978), London, Hutchinson, 1972. Its list of illustrations, which the item page shows without borrowing, is a roll-call: «Major-General Robert D'Arcy, R.E., C.B.», «Jean D'Arcy, nee Ward», «Colonel Joseph D'Arcy, R.A.», «Lady Catherine D'Arcy, nee West», «The Three Aunts D'Arcy, JANE, KATE AND CHARLOTTE», one of those aunts «in Persian dress BROUGHT HOME BY HER BROTHER JOSEPH», «George Abbas Kooli D'Arcy», «Robert West D'Arcy», «Annie Hewish D'Arcy, nee Adams» — and then «Amy Darwin, nee Ruck» and «Charles Darwin». PHOTOGRAPHS OF NINE OF THESE PEOPLE WERE PRINTED IN 1972.

AND IT HAS BEEN HIDING UNDER A TYPING ERROR FOR FIFTY YEARS. The Internet Archive catalogues it under the subject «DORSEY FAMILY», which is a cataloguer's mangling of D'Arcy, so no search for the surname has ever surfaced it. The GEDCOM notes this archive inherited quote «by Berta Ruck» in two places and NOBODY HAD ASKED WHO SHE WAS. The answer took one search: FreeBMD gives «RUCK, Arthur Ashley» and «D'ARCY, Elizabeth Eleanor» AT THE SAME VOLUME AND PAGE — Penzance, September quarter 1877, GRO 5c 381, in a quarter marked >99% transcribed. Berta was born the following year. The tree asserted a Ruck connection; THIS IS THE FIRST RECORD OF IT.

THE BOOK ALSO SETTLES A NAME THE TREE COULD NOT DECIDE. The GEDCOM hedged «Anne Heevish or Hewish Adams» for the wife Robert West D'Arcy married at Bombay in 1846. THREE RECORDS NOW AGREE AND NONE OF THEM COPIED THE OTHERS: the India Office ecclesiastical return indexes her ANNE H ADAMS, the Gentleman's Magazine announcement calls her ANNIE ADAMS, and her great-niece's plate list names her ANNIE HEWISH D'ARCY, NEE ADAMS. An initial in a government index, a forename in a magazine, and a caption under a photograph, and between them a woman has her whole name back.

WHAT IS NOT CLAIMED. That Berta Ruck is the daughter of that 1877 marriage is AN INFERENCE FROM A DATE AND A FATHER'S NAME, not a record, and whose daughter Elizabeth Eleanor was is not established at all. The «C.B.» after Robert D'Arcy's name is a caption written by a descendant in 1972, not an official list, and is recorded as a lead to test against the Gazette rather than an honour this archive has documented. The book's text is in copyright and lending-restricted: ONLY THE PLATE LIST WAS READ, BORROWING NEEDS AN ACCOUNT AND NONE WAS MADE, and reading it properly is now on the work list as something a library copy would solve.

ONE SEARCH WAS RUN THAT COULD NEVER HAVE ANSWERED, AND IS WRITTEN DOWN FOR THAT REASON. Births to a Ruck father with a D'Arcy mother, 1878-1900, returned nothing — because THE GRO BIRTH INDEX DOES NOT CARRY THE MOTHER'S MAIDEN NAME UNTIL SEPTEMBER 1911. The zero is the shape of the index and not a fact about anybody. After two days of finding instruments that answer a different question from the one asked, this archive can at least recognise one of its own.

AND THE SAME SEARCH REACHED THE OLDEST QUESTION ON THESE PAGES. The Internet Archive's full text carries NOTES AND QUERIES for 1 DECEMBER 1866, page 432, where a correspondent asks «who was the grandfather of MAJOR-GENERAL ROBERT D'ARCY, R.E., WHO DIED COMMANDANT OF CHATHAM IN 1827?» and prints, as FAMILY TRADITION, the answer this archive has spent months disputing: «Colonel d'Arcy, A BRANCH OF THE HOLDERNESS FAMILY FROM YORKSHIRE, commanded a regiment during the American War. He was KILLED IN ACTION, leaving two sons: 1. Robert, Major-General R.E. 2. CONSTANTINE, Lieut. R.A., DIED S.P. On his voyage to America Colonel d'Arcy and his family were WRECKED. They lost all their baggage and papers, which, it is believed, would have proved their noble descent.»

THREE THINGS MAKE THAT WORTH MORE THAN THE STORY IT CARRIES. It is ONE HUNDRED AND FIFTY-NINE YEARS OLDER than the family tree that states Yorkshire as a fact, so the tree did not invent it and nor did MyHeritage. The man who printed it was ASKING, NOT ASSERTING — he wanted the grandfather and did not have him. And THE EXCUSE FOR THE MISSING EVIDENCE IS INSIDE THE STORY: a shipwreck that drowned exactly the papers which would have proved the descent, which is the shape a pedigree takes when it cannot be documented. A full-text search for «Commandant of Chatham» returns 144 hits across everything the Internet Archive holds and the only one in Notes and Queries is the question itself. NOBODY EVER ANSWERED IT. The question has stood open in print since 1866 and this archive has now joined the queue.

IT ALSO HANDS OVER THE FIRST TESTABLE THING THE TRADITION HAS EVER OFFERED. A man who COMMANDED A BRITISH REGIMENT AND DIED IN ACTION between 1775 and 1783 is not obscure: he is in the Army Lists, his death is gazetted and his successor is gazetted after him. A first pass found nine «Arcy» notices in the Gazette for 1775-1790 and the officers in them are a Brevet Major FRANCIS D'Arcy and an Ensign JOHN POMEROY D'Arcy — no colonel. THAT IS NOT A DISPROOF AND IS NOT FILED AS ONE: this archive has watched the same Gazette OCR turn the surname into «D'Aroy» inside a single career, and the site will not page past its first ten results. The Army Lists themselves are free and full-text on the Internet Archive, and the work list now says so.

AND THE GOVERNOR GOVERNED TWICE. A Falkland Islands bibliography and Henige's Colonial Governors between them give «Colonel George Abbas Kooli D'Arcy: GOVERNOR OF THE FALKLAND ISLANDS 1870-1876», after the Gambia from 1859 — two colonies and the Atlantic between them, and this archive knew of neither until this week. The same search finally identified the «military records for 1840 and 1841» that have sat on the work list as a bare phrase: they are the MONTHLY ARMY LISTS OF 1840, which print «Adj. Geo. Abbas Kooli [D']Arcy» and confirm he was ADJUTANT of the 94th. Notes and Queries adds, in 1866, that he was then «THE PRESENT REPRESENTATIVE OF THE FAMILY», claiming descent from Edward III THROUGH HIS MOTHER — Catherine Georgiana West — with arms and a crest. A claim reported, not a pedigree proved, and graded accordingly.

AND THEN THE TRADITION WAS TESTED, THE SAME DAY IT WAS FOUND, AND IT SPLIT CLEANLY IN TWO. Four official Army Lists — 1775, 1776, 1778 and 1783, lists of GENERAL AND FIELD OFFICERS — were downloaded and searched entire. THE TWO SONS ARE BOTH THERE. The 1783 volume puts ROBERT D'ARCEY in THE CORPS OF ENGINEERS, among the lieutenants, in a block of officers all dated 17 JANUARY 1776 — THE EXACT DATE THIS ARCHIVE ALREADY HELD for his first commission, printed seven years later and reached by a different road. And it puts CONSTANT[INE] D'ARCEY, 12 July, among the FIRST LIEUTENANTS OF THE ROYAL REGIMENT OF ARTILLERY, which is word for word what the tradition claimed: «Constantine, Lieut. R.A.»

THE COLONEL IS IN NONE OF THEM. No Colonel D'Arcy appears in 1775, 1776, 1778 or 1783. The only officers of the surname are Francis D'Arcy, John Pomeroy D'Arcy, and a George and a John in the indexes. THE CONTROL IS THE VOLUMES THEMSELVES: they use the word «Colonel» 230, 235, 245 and 312 times, so they are not silent about colonels. THREE GAPS KEEP IT SHORT OF A DISPROOF and are stated rather than buried — a provincial or loyalist colonel need not be listed, nor one on the Irish establishment, and «Colonel» may have been a local or courtesy rank. BUT THE SHAPE IS HARD TO MISS. A tradition recorded in 1866 is right about the two men it names who can be checked, and silent of support for the one man it needs. THE SHIPWRECK THAT DROWNED THE PAPERS WAS DOING A LOT OF WORK IN 1866 AND IT IS DOING IT STILL.

AND THE DEPARTMENT THAT APPOINTED HIM HAD WRITTEN HIS LIFE DOWN ALL ALONG. The Colonial Office List for 1877 is free, out of copyright, and its whole text is a single 2.2 MB file. Its biographical notice runs: adjutant of the 94th for three years, SIXTEEN YEARS IN THAT CORPS; AUTHOR OF A WORK ON «LIGHT INFANTRY DRILL»; commanded the 3rd West India Regiment for several years; served in the SOUTHERN MAHRATTA AND SAWANT-WARREE CAMPAIGN OF 1845-6 UNDER BRIGADIER OUTRAM; AIDE-DE-CAMP AND ASSISTANT PRIVATE SECRETARY TO FIVE SUCCESSIVE GOVERNORS OF BOMBAY and to Sir Willoughby Cotton commanding the Bombay army; SOLD OUT IN 1858; Governor and Commander-in-Chief of the Gambia from JUNE 1859; an expedition against the robber-king of BADDIBOO that earned him the thanks of the Secretary of State; the BATTLE OF SABBA, 21 FEBRUARY 1861.

AND A VICTORIA CROSS WAS WON FOLLOWING HIM THROUGH A STOCKADE. At Tubabecolong in 1866 he embarked at FORTY-EIGHT HOURS' NOTICE against a Marabout invasion and carried the entrenched position. TWO OFFICERS WERE KILLED AT HIS SIDE — Lieutenants Kelly and Jenkins of the 4th West India Regiment — with four soldiers, two volunteers, four of the native contingent and sixty-one of all ranks badly wounded. «PRIVATE SAMUEL HODGE, WHO FOLLOWED COLONEL D'ARCY THROUGH THE STOCKADE, RECEIVED THE VICTORIA CROSS.» Hodge was among the first black soldiers to receive it. On leaving the Gambia in January 1867 the European merchants gave him a sword of honour worth £120. ONE EDITORIAL CHOICE IS ON THE RECORD: the 1877 entry describes the invaders in the racial language of its period and that phrase is not reproduced here, because nothing in this family's history turns on it.

AND IT QUIETLY EXPLAINS THE BOMBAY MARRIAGE. George was aide-de-camp to five governors of Bombay and campaigning in the Southern Mahratta country in 1845-6. HIS BROTHER ROBERT WEST MARRIED ANNIE HEWISH ADAMS AT BOMBAY ON 20 JANUARY 1846. That is an observation and it is filed as one: NO SOURCE PLACES THE TWO BROTHERS IN THE SAME ROOM, only in the same presidency in the same months. But the archive now knows why there were D'Arcys in Bombay at all, which it did not on Thursday.

AND THE BOOK THIS ARCHIVE HAS BEEN CITING FOR MONTHS HAD NEVER BEEN READ. Porter's History of the Corps of Royal Engineers was in the sources as «Porter's station list», the authority for Robert D'Arcy being posted to Barbados. ITS INDEX GIVES HIM THREE CAMPAIGNS: «D'ARCY, Robert, at second siege of MINORCA, 209, 216; COPENHAGEN, 243; WALCHEREN, 248.» At MINORCA he is one of six Engineer officers inside Fort St Philip's when the Duc de Crillon landed on 19 August 1781 — a garrison of three thousand, besieged six months. At WALCHEREN in 1809 he is something else entirely: of five corps in an army of forty thousand under the Earl of Chatham, the largest was Sir Eyre Coote's, and «THE COMMANDING ROYAL ENGINEER WITH THIS CORPS WAS LIEUTENANT-COLONEL R. D'ARCY». JOSEPH'S OBITUARY, HELD HERE SINCE SEPTEMBER, SAYS JOSEPH WAS AT THE TAKING OF WALCHEREN TOO — the father commanding the Engineers of the main corps, the son a Royal Artillery officer of twenty-nine, and neither record knows about the other.

HE WAS ALSO PUT UNDER ARREST THERE, AND THE REASON IS THE ONLY PIECE OF HIS CHARACTER THIS ARCHIVE HAS. Colonel Fyers, shot through the chest at Flushing, ordered the senior engineer in the trenches to hand in a written report every morning. The Brigade-Major wrote it down: «The first morning, Colonel D., AN OLD MAN BEYOND SIXTY, refused compliance, saying HE HAD OTHER THINGS TO DO, and no solicitation could prevail on him to write a single line.» The third morning he refused again, «SAYING IT WAS ALL NONSENSE», and denied his superior's right to ask him for anything «BECAUSE SOME THIRTY OR FORTY YEARS PREVIOUSLY HE HAD BEEN SENIOR TO COLONEL F.» He was arrested; the preliminaries of a court-martial were gone through; and then he «thought better of it, made his apologies, was released, and ever after furnished his report». Porter names him only in a footnote.

AND THE INSULT CARRIES A DATE. «AN OLD MAN BEYOND SIXTY» IN AUGUST 1809 PUTS HIS BIRTH BEFORE ABOUT 1749. The family tree says 1751, which would have made him fifty-eight that summer and not «beyond sixty». IT IS AN EYEWITNESS IMPRESSION PRINTED EIGHTY YEARS LATER AND NOT A REGISTER, and it is graded as that. But the tree's 1751 is itself only arithmetic from an age on a burial register, so this is now TWO SOFT NUMBERS DISAGREEING rather than one standing unopposed — and it is the sort of thing /hornby exists to keep track of.

AND THE SAME TRICK WAS TURNED ON THE OLDEST QUESTION IN THE ENGLISH LINE. Item 106 has been asking for THE BERKELEY REGISTER ITSELF since September, because every index has failed. PHILLIMORE'S «GLOUCESTERSHIRE PARISH REGISTERS: MARRIAGES» IS A PRINTED TRANSCRIPT SERIES, free and out of copyright, and A TRANSCRIPT IS THE REGISTER. Six volumes were downloaded whole and read. They print Ampney Crucis, Naunton, Prestbury, Sevenhampton, Thornbury, Kingscote, Painswick, Batsford, Beverston, Ebrington, Elkstone, Standish, Stinchcombe, Weston Birt, Willersey, Stone and Nether Swell. BERKELEY IS NOT AMONG THEM — every «Berkeley» in the text is a bride or groom described as «of Berkeley» in somebody else's parish. No John Saniger marries any Lydia in any of the six, against a control of THIRTY-SIX SANIGAR MARRIAGES PRINTED ACROSS THE SERIES, so the surname is in no way invisible to it.

ONE THING FELL OUT OF IT THAT NO PAGE HERE HAS EVER SAID. THE SURNAME IS THICKEST AT STONE, the parish adjoining Berkeley — twenty of the thirty-six entries, in the 1670s to 1690s, with the rest at Thornbury, Cam and Dursley. This archive's Sanigars are at Berkeley and Ham and it has never asked where the name itself lives. IT IS DISTRIBUTION AND NOT DESCENT, and is recorded as that: not one of the thirty-six is shown to be a relative of anybody here.

Allen's Indian Mail reported his death at Bangor in 1862, having printed his marriage twice in 1846
FIBIS — ten of the twelve sources a default search returned were soundex ghosts, not D'Arcys
/worklist 106 — FreeREG cannot answer Lydia's marriage, and a MARY control proves the zero is coverage

did: OWN ERROR 56, AND IT IS THE FOURTH OF ITS EXACT SHAPE IN TWO DAYS. Yesterday this archive published that TWELVE citations no longer lead anywhere, «four of them FamilySearch collection URLs this archive chose itself, which makes them the worst four on the list». ALL FOUR ARE ALIVE AND ALWAYS WERE. urllib sends no Accept header unless it is told to, and FamilySearch answers a request without one with a flat 404. The rewrite of check_cites.py the day before had already caught three faults of precisely this kind — a swallowed backslash, a 302 graded as a refusal, a wrapped DNS error — and then shipped a fourth, because the tool was tested against what it reported rather than against what a reader sees. OPENING ONE OF THE DEAD ONES IN A BROWSER TOOK UNDER A MINUTE AND WAS NOT DONE BEFORE PUBLISHING.

WITH THE HEADER SENT THE PICTURE IS BETTER THAN THE ONE THAT WAS PUBLISHED, AND THE GOOD NEWS IS THE PART THAT MATTERS. 300 RESOLVE, 264 WALLED, 6 TIMED OUT, 4 HOSTS GONE, 5 REFUSED. NINE candidates for a dead citation, and EVERY ONE OF THE NINE WAS INHERITED FROM THE GEDCOM EXPORT — they appear only in families.json, ancestors.json and line.json, which are built from the MyHeritage file. NOT ONE CITATION THIS ARCHIVE CHOSE FOR ITSELF IS DEAD. The nine are three links into the AIF Project and one to Brisbane's grave search, neither hostname resolving any more; two to a personal genealogy site; a Familypedia page on the old wikia.com domain; an Australharmony page at Sydney; and an EMPTY WAR MEMORIAL SEARCH URL, which is a search box somebody saved rather than a citation at all.

AND THE TOOL NOW DRAWS THAT LINE ITSELF RATHER THAN LEAVING IT TO WHOEVER READS THE OUTPUT. check_cites.py marks every dead link «OURS» or «inherited» and closes with «of those, 0 are citations THIS ARCHIVE CHOSE and 9 were inherited from the GEDCOM export. Only the first number is anybody's job here.» NOTHING IS BEING REPAIRED AND NOTHING DELETED: mending another person's footnote inside an inherited file would make it look like this archive's work and would be overwritten by the next export.

THE MARRIAGE HAS SAT HERE SINCE AUGUST AS A BARE FACT WITH THE WORDS «TRANSCRIPT PAYWALLED EVEN ON A PAID TRIAL». Robert West D'Arcy, second son of Joseph, married at Bombay in 1846 and that was all this archive could say. FIBIS — the FAMILIES IN BRITISH INDIA SOCIETY database, free, indexing India Office material, and never opened here — names her twice from two separate indexes. The Gentleman's Magazine marriage announcements: «ROBERT WEST D'ARCY × ANNIE ADAMS, 20 JANUARY 1846, BOMBAY». The Index of Ecclesiastical returns, IOR BOMBAY MARRIAGES: «Husband ROBT WEST D'ARCY · Wife ANNE H ADAMS, 1846». TWO INDEXES, ONE MARRIAGE, AND HER NAME SPELLED TWO WAYS BY PEOPLE WHO WERE NOT COPYING EACH OTHER. The day comes from the magazine; the India Office return gives only the year.

AND THE ANGLO-INDIAN PRESS FOLLOWED HIM HOME TO WALES. Allen's Indian Mail printed the Bombay marriage twice in 1846 — once as «Robert W.», once as «Robert West» — and then, sixteen years later, «D'ARCY, Robert · BANGOR, N.WALES · 1862». This archive already had the English notice of that death, «late of the Honourable East India Company's Army, dead at Bangor on 14 June». Now the India side of his life records the same death from the other direction, which is what ties the Bangor man to the Company officer without anybody having to assume it.

WHAT FIBIS DID NOT GIVE IS THE THING THE ERRAND WAS OPENED FOR. There is no cadet paper, no commission, no medal roll entry and no child. The India Office papers at the British Library remain the document that would give birth, parentage and career together, and nothing here replaces them.

AND THE COUNT THAT LOOKED LIKE A HARVEST WAS MOSTLY GHOSTS. A default FIBIS search for «Robert D'Arcy» returns TWELVE SOURCES, which reads like twelve findings. THE DEFAULT IS SOUNDEX, AND ON THIS SURNAME IT MATCHES TRACY, TRACEY, TRAISE, DRUCE AND D'ROSE. The «Gentleman's Magazine death announcement for Robert D'Arcy» is Robert Alexander DRUCE, dead in 1829. The «Register of European Soldiers, Bengal Army» entry is Robert TRACY, gunner. Both Indian Mutiny Medal Roll hits are Tracey and Traise. The five «CMB» entries are a D'Rose family at Lucknow in the 1920s. TEN OF TWELVE. A RESULT COUNT FROM THIS DATABASE IS NOT A COUNT OF ANYTHING UNTIL THE ROWS ARE OPENED, and the same search set to exact returns 29 sources for D'Arcy in the whole database, which is the figure worth quoting.

ONE MORE ROUTE TO LYDIA CLOSED, AND CLOSED PROPERLY. Every earlier attempt at her maiden name went through FindMyPast. FREEREG IS A SEPARATE TRANSCRIPTION PROJECT WITH SEPARATE COVERAGE AND HAD NEVER BEEN ASKED. It cannot answer either, and the three parishes that matter fail in three different ways: BERKELEY holds 2,916 records and the whole run is 1600–1677, stopping a hundred and twenty years short; WOTTON-UNDER-EDGE, where she was born, holds 16,105 and STARTS AT 1813; THORNBURY spans the 1790s and looked like the way in. A search of Thornbury AND UP TO A HUNDRED NEARBY PARISHES for any Lydia marrying 1790–1805 returns nothing — AND SO DOES THE SAME SEARCH FOR ANY MARY. That control is the whole value of the exercise: zero Marys marrying across a hundred parishes in sixteen years is not a fact about Gloucestershire, it is the absence of transcribed marriages, and without it the Lydia zero would have looked like evidence.

AND WHETHER THE GOVERNOR OF THE GAMBIA EVER MARRIED IS ASKED AND NOT ANSWERED. FreeBMD holds FOUR George D'Arcy marriages in England and Wales across 1837–1890 — Norwich 1864, Westminster 1884, Hackney 1888, West Ham 1889 — in quarters FreeBMD itself marks >99% transcribed, and NONE CARRIES HIS FORENAMES. The GRO index records every forename a man registered under and a «George Abbas Kooli» does not hide as a plain «George». IT IS A WEAK NULL AND IS FILED AS ONE: all four results fall in September quarters, which across four records deserves somebody's second look, and he spent most of his adult life outside English registration altogether — the 94th Foot, the 3rd West India Regiment from 1852, the Gambia from 1859. A marriage at Bathurst would not be in this index at all.

AND THE WORK LIST WAS TELLING A FLATTERING LIE ABOUT ITSELF. Its own definitions are plain: NEXT MEANS READY TO START, BLOCKED MEANS WAITING ON A PERSON OR AN INSTITUTION. Eight items sat under «next» and five of them had not been ready to start for weeks — Barbados, which its own note said in September needed the originals; Lydia, which needs the Berkeley register or the diocesan bonds; Joseph's sons, which now need the India Office cadet papers and a Gambia register; Margaret's baptism and the Ruabon baptism, both of which need a register image after today's measurements closed the free indexes. ALL FIVE ARE NOW BLOCKED AND EACH SAYS WHAT IT IS WAITING FOR. A list that calls a wall «next» is a list that makes the archive look busier than it is.

WHAT IS LEFT UNDER «NEXT» IS THREE ITEMS AND ONLY ONE IS THIS ARCHIVE'S. Two belong to other sessions in the estate — the Luwinski and Our Family work lists, and the shared kit's gazetteer. The third is WELSH NEWSPAPERS ONLINE, tried three times across two days and stopped every time by the same Cloudflare interstitial. IT STAYS «NEXT» DELIBERATELY RATHER THAN BEING FILED AS BLOCKED: it is free, it wants no account and no fee, nobody has to write a letter or pay anybody, and somebody with an ordinary browser will open it in one click. Nothing is waiting on a person or an institution — only on a bot check that dislikes this browser, and that is not the same kind of wall.
