did: THE ACTS WERE READ, AND THE THING THIS PAGE HAS WANTED FOR A MONTH IS AN AGE. Margaret Jones née D'Arcy died at SIX IN THE MORNING ON 1 FEBRUARY 1843, at her house in the rue de l'Hôpital, Ingouville, AGED SIXTY-ONE — which puts her birth about 1781. It is the FIRST DATING OF A CHILD OF ROBERT D'ARCY THAT COMES FROM A RECORD rather than from a tree. Her husband died seven weeks later, on 21 MARCH, at eight in the morning in the rue du Champ de Foire, AGED SIXTY-EIGHT, born about 1774. Each act names the other person: hers calls her his wife, his calls him her widower. A marriage entered at Chatham in 1806 is confirmed in 1843 by French clerks who had never heard of Chatham and spelled both names by ear — «Maddack», «Marguéritta Maria Elisabella Darcy».

AND NEITHER ACT CAN CARRY ROBERT D'ARCY, WHICH IS THE POINT OF THE ERRAND AND IS NOT ANSWERED. Both record the birthplace of the dead person as unknown, and his adds that the names of his father and mother are unknown too. The declarants were four neighbours — a police appariteur of twenty-two, a farmer of forty-eight, two men of private means of fifty-nine and fifty-eight — and every act notes that they were NOT RELATIVES. Two English people in their sixties had died in a French suburb among people who did not know where either of them came from. The D'Arcy parentage still rests where it rested, on the English notices. ERRAND 35 IS MARKED ANSWERED FOR THE AGE AND SAYS IN ITS OWN ENTRY THAT THE PARENTAGE IT WAS OPENED FOR IS STILL OPEN.

OWN ERROR 55. A DÉCENNALE TABLE WAS READ RIGHT THROUGH FOR THE WRONG INGOUVILLE. Cote 4 E 10127 was picked out of the search results for being the smallest index — forty-eight views — and its 1843–1852 décès table was paged to the J section and read: nine entries, Jean, Jouette, Junais, and no Jones. The verdict was worthless. TWO THINGS ON THE SCREEN SAID SO AND NEITHER WAS READ. The image URL filed the volume under «ingouville-sur-mer», a village near Saint-Valery-en-Caux sixty kilometres up the coast. And forty-eight views cannot hold thirty years of births, marriages and deaths for a town of fifteen thousand — the right table, 4 E 9933, spends THREE HUNDRED AND NINE VIEWS ON ONE DECADE. The surnames gave it away too, had anyone asked: Jouette, Blanquet, Barthélemy. A REGISTER IS NOT IDENTIFIED BY ITS TITLE. It is identified by its provenance and its size, and both were on the page.

THE ACT WAS FOUND BY DATE, NOT BY INDEX, WHICH IS WHY THE WRONG TABLE COST NOTHING IN THE END. The 1843 deaths register of Ingouville, 4 E 9077, runs chronologically at about two acts to a view, so a known date is a binary search: act 116 is 23 March, act 85 is 1 March, act 65 is 16 February. Jones's death on the 21st had to be act 113, and it is. Margaret's was narrowed by her own notice — the Morning Herald printed it on 13 February, so the death was days earlier — and act 43 is the first of the month. THE INDEX WAS NEVER NEEDED.

AND THE PAGE THAT GRADES EVERYTHING ELSE HAD A NUMBER NOBODY WAS GRADING. /errands carried the heading «50 OPEN · 8 ANSWERED AND KEPT» as a hand-typed string in its data, while the rows under it held FIFTY-TWO AND FOURTEEN. The page already had a counting helper and was not using it for the heading. A count that is retyped is a claim that can go stale in silence, which is the one failure this archive builds gates against — so the eyebrow is now computed from the rows, and answering an errand cannot leave the heading behind. The same tally on /changes was already computed; its data file carried a dead stale copy, which is gone.

THE ARCHIVE'S IMAGES WERE READ THROUGH THE BROWSER, NOT SCRIPTED. The Seine-Maritime viewer serves IIIF, and a first pass pulled page crops with curl until the server began returning placeholder tiles. The browser held a «techaro.lol-anubis-auth» cookie — a proof-of-work token earned by passing a bot check. Replaying that token outside the browser would have been working around the gate, so the scripting stopped there and the rest of the reading was done by navigating the browser to the crops, which is what the viewer itself does. THE RULE IS NOT «GET THE IMAGES»; IT IS «DO NOT DEFEAT A BOT GATE», AND IT COST NOTHING TO KEEP.

AND THE AGE TURNED OUT TO CONFIRM SOMETHING NOBODY HAD CHECKED. This archive already carried 26 SEPTEMBER 1781, PORTSMOUTH for Margaret's birth — out of the family tree, never matched to a record, and sitting in a table beside her brother's documented one. A woman born that day is SIXTY-ONE YEARS AND FOUR MONTHS OLD on 1 February 1843, which is exactly the age the act gives. The two men who gave it were neighbours who did not know her birthplace or her parents, and said so in the same sentence. They could not have known the date and they confirmed it. It also seats her in the family: Joseph was born 14 March 1780, she is eighteen months behind him, and the 1806 notice calls her the ELDEST DAUGHTER. Three statements, none written with the others in view.

A REDISCOVERY WAS CAUGHT BEFORE IT WAS PUBLISHED, AND IT IS WORTH RECORDING THAT IT WAS NEARLY NOT. Sweeping FreeREG for a D'Arcy daughter turned up JOSEPH D'ARCY, BAPTISED PORTSEA ST MARY 19 MARCH 1780, FATHER ROBERT, MOTHER JEAN — which reads like the first parish record naming Robert D'Arcy as a father, and was written up in this session's head as exactly that. IT IS ALREADY IN THE REGISTER, CITED TO FREEREG, with the Hampshire Genealogical Society's independent transcription beside it. The archive's own «memory» error class has ten entries and every one of them is this: announcing as new something already held. The eleventh was avoided by reading build_register.py before writing a word, which took under a minute and should not have been optional.

WHAT THE SWEEP DID BUY IS A MEASURED FLOOR UNDER WORK LIST 142. Portsea St Mary's whole FreeREG holding is 992 RECORDS, ALL BAPTISMS, 1780–1782 — so a baptism of September 1781 would be inside it, and Hampshire returns Joseph alone on both exact and loose spellings. Portsmouth St Thomas holds 9,079 records, ALL MARRIAGES, 1651–1776, and no baptisms at any date. Old Portsmouth holds nothing. Nationally there are eighteen exact D'Arcy baptisms between 1775 and 1790 and the only Margaret among them is at Happisburgh in January 1775, which would make her sixty-eight at death rather than sixty-one. The next step is a register image, not another index.

AND A SEARCH NOBODY SHOULD REPEAT. WORK LIST 143 WANTED A RUABON BAPTISM FOR JOHN MADDOCK JONES ABOUT 1774. FreeREG holds 30,976 transcriptions for RUABON ST MARY and the baptism column is BLANK FOR THE 1770s, 1780s, 1790s AND 1800s, starting at 1,078 in 1810–1819 — while those same 1770s carry 253 marriages and 722 burials. The original register begins in 1559; it is the transcription that stops. The Welsh-named duplicate place «Rhiwabon» in the same county list is an empty stub and not a second chance. On Welsh custom his middle name should be his mother's maiden surname, so Denbighshire was swept for MADDOCK across 1750–1785: EIGHTY-SEVEN RECORDS AND NONE AT RUABON, with ten Ruabon rows returned in the same result set to prove the parish was in scope. Three Jones–Maddock marriages exist in the county and the nearest in date, Gresford in January 1772, IS A RESEMBLANCE AND IS ATTACHED TO NOBODY.

A NATIONAL LIBRARY THE ATLAS DID NOT HAVE. Looking for a free copy of the Caernarvon & Denbigh Herald obituary this archive cites through a paywall led to WELSH NEWSPAPERS ONLINE, free and covering 1804–1919 — and to the discovery that the Record Atlas listed NO WELSH PROVIDER AT ALL except Findmypast and the GRO, both paid. The National Library of Wales is now a row there. Its newspaper service did not open today: a Cloudflare «Performing security verification» interstitial that did not clear in about forty seconds, on the search URL and on the bare homepage. IT WAS NOT WORKED AROUND, the Library's main site loaded normally in the same session, and the access class was left «unsurveyed» rather than guessed from one browser on one day.

AND THE LINK CHECKER WAS NOT SLOW, IT WAS WRONG. check_cites.py has existed for weeks, wired into nothing, and the reason on record was speed: 581 URLs one at a time, no output until the last returned, a run abandoned at eight minutes. That was the smaller fault. IT READ STATUS CODES AND NOTHING ELSE, and myheritage.com — 428 of the 581, carried in from the GEDCOM export rather than chosen here — ANSWERS A ROBOT WITH HTTP 200 AND AN 843-BYTE BODY READING «Request unsuccessful. Incapsula incident ID: …». Every one of them would have been counted as a healthy citation. The headline would have been confident, reassuring and wrong about three quarters of what this archive cites. A STATUS CODE IS NOT A PAGE; the rewrite reads the first four kilobytes and calls that outcome «walled», which is neither alive nor dead but is what is true.

RUNNING IT PROPERLY FOUND THREE MORE BUGS, ALL IN THE DIRECTION OF CRYING WOLF. Ten URLs had swallowed a trailing backslash out of JSON escaping and one had swallowed an «&nbsp», so «nla.gov.au/nla.news-article3635563\» came back 404 and the tool was INVENTING dead citations. 436 MyHeritage 302s were being graded «refused» and printed under a heading that invited somebody to read them as dead. And urllib.error.URLError WRAPS the name-resolution failure rather than letting socket.gaierror through, so a host that does not exist was filed beside a host that was merely slow. A report that is read is a report that does not cry wolf, and this one would have cried wolf eleven times before it said anything true.

IT IS NOW IN THE BUILD, AT A TENTH OF A SECOND. The network sweep is a separate deliberate run of about two minutes; the build reads a committed cache, prints how old the numbers are, and says so in its own voice past sixty days — because a cache is a measurement with a date on it and goes stale without ever looking wrong. The tally that day: 105 RESOLVE, 428 REDIRECT, 26 WALLED, 6 TIMED OUT ON THIS MACHINE, 4 HOSTS GONE, 8 REFUSED — TWELVE CANDIDATES, AND THE NUMBER WAS WRONG. See 10 October: urllib sends no Accept header unless told to, four of the twelve were alive, and the real figure is NINE, none of them a citation this archive chose. OWN ERROR 56.

SUPERSEDED THE NEXT MORNING, AND BADLY. This entry said four of the twelve dead links were FamilySearch collection URLs chosen by this archive, “which makes them the worst four on the list”. ALL FOUR WERE ALIVE. The checker was not sending an Accept header and FamilySearch answers a request without one with a flat 404. What survives is the other half: graves.brisbane.qld.gov.au and three links into the AIF Project at aif.adfa.edu.au genuinely no longer resolve as hostnames — and all of those were INHERITED FROM THE GEDCOM EXPORT too. Own error 56, on /corrections.

AND THE LAST THING THE DAY FOUND WAS A COLONIAL GOVERNOR. Work list 134 wanted to know «which corps, which rank» for GEORGE ABBAS KOOLI D'ARCY, Joseph's eldest son, baptised at Westminster in 1818 and known to this archive only from «military records for 1840 and 1841» and a death in Devon in 1885. THE GAZETTE HAS TEN NOTICES ON HIM AND IT IS FREE AND THIS ARCHIVE ALREADY CITES IT. Ensign in the 94TH REGIMENT OF FOOT by April 1837 — the notice exists only to correct the War Office: «The Christian names of Ensign D'Arcy, of the 94th Regiment of Foot, are George Abbas Kooli». Lieutenant 1839. Captain 1846. Major of the 3RD WEST INDIA REGIMENT in 1852, «from the 94th Foot». Lieutenant-Colonel 1854. And on 17 JUNE 1859: «COLONEL GEORGE ABBAS KOOLI D'ARCY TO BE GOVERNOR AND COMMANDER-IN-CHIEF IN AND OVER HER MAJESTY'S SETTLEMENTS IN THE RIVER GAMBIA», gazetted in the same sentence as the new Governor of Hong Kong.

THE IDENTIFICATION DOES NOT REST ON THE NAME BEING ODD, THOUGH IT IS THE ODDEST IN THIS ARCHIVE. It rests on something already on these pages: ABBAS KOOLY IS ABBAS QOLI, FOR PRINCE ABBAS MIRZA, WHOM HIS FATHER HAD SERVED FIVE YEARS IN PERSIA — which comes out of Joseph's own obituary, found weeks before anybody looked for the son's career. A boy baptised at Westminster on 31 August 1818 is eighteen when the War Office gazettes him an Ensign in the spring of 1837. The name is not a coincidence to be explained away; it is the evidence, and the thing it points at was already documented here.

AND THE SEARCH WORKED FOR A REASON WORTH WRITING DOWN. The Gazette's OCR mangles him freely — «Qeorge», «Greorge», «D'Aroy» — so a search on the surname would have missed most of it, and a search on the forename would have drowned. KOOLI SURVIVES EVERY MANGLING BECAUSE NOTHING ELSE IN THE CORPUS LOOKS LIKE IT. Ten is a floor rather than a ceiling: an OCR slip could still be hiding a later notice, nothing after 1859 was found, and WHETHER HE EVER MARRIED IS STILL UNANSWERED. One 1857 notice lists him among officers of mixed rank each with a date; THE HEADING OVER THAT LIST WAS NOT READ, so what it conferred is not claimed — only that he is a Colonel by 1859.

days.title: The research reached the pages and left four people behind, and split two more in half
found: /errands 35 — the two 1843 deaths at Havre have a free French route, never tried, and it is not Kew
/sanigers — three Sanigar burials at Kingswood, and a coordinate settling which Kingswood
every gate, for one that answers a different question from the one it reports — and found a tool that asks nobody
/coverage — the BillionGraves correction was itself wrong. Four English Sanigars, not none. Own error 54
/coverage — BillionGraves was never blocked. Own error 53
the charts again — Joseph D'Arcy's five Milford children, Charlotte at Chatham, Jane at Barbados. 41 edges became 54
/graves and /households now publish what the tree does not carry, as /marriages does — 26 and 8
the charts — 6 more documented parent links drawn; 41 edges became 47
the atlas and the timeline — the timeline is honest, the atlas cannot map seven documented places
/marriages said «every marriage this archive can date» and showed only the tree's. 34 documented ones were missing
/people/miriam-wakefield — her death registration and her sworn deposition were on two other pages
/who/catherine-georgiana-west — one woman, two dossiers, half her evidence on each
/who — Catherine Sneyd, James Sanigar and Laura Sayer, documented for weeks and carried by nothing
did: AND THE BEST FIND OF THE DAY CAME OUT OF A THROWAWAY LINE. The Record Atlas session mentioned eight French departmental archives that refuse a script and open to a browser. This archive has TWO DEATHS IN FRANCE — Margaret Jones née D'Arcy at Havre in February 1843 and her husband Major John Maddock Jones at Ingouville in March — and had pursued both ONLY through British consular returns at Kew, which are «miscellaneous» by their own title. NO FRENCH ARCHIVE HAD EVER BEEN TRIED.

THE SEINE-MARITIME ARCHIVE IS OPEN, FREE, AND HOLDS THE REGISTERS. Its first response was a «Making sure you're not a bot!» interstitial that resolved by itself — precisely the behaviour reported. Ingouville, décès, 1843 returns five results including THE COMPLETE YEAR'S DEATHS REGISTER, COTE 4 E 9077, 310 VIEWS, with two tables décennales over it. Le Havre returns twelve, covering the town and the communes it absorbed. A French death act carries the age, the birthplace, the parents and the surviving spouse — MORE THAN THE CONSULAR RETURN THIS ARCHIVE WAS QUEUEING FOR, and for Margaret that is the nearest thing to a birth date for a daughter of Robert D'Arcy. Work list 141: read them, tables décennales first.

AND BACK TO RESEARCH, BECAUSE THE DAY HAD FOUND FOUR OWN ERRORS AND NO ANCESTORS. The newly-opened source was asked a positive question, which is the one it can answer. HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, KINGSWOOD HOLDS THREE SANIGAR BURIALS — Andrew 1980, Dennis 2003, Barbara 2008 — and the cemetery page settles which Kingswood with a coordinate: 51.4616, -2.5033, which is KINGSWOOD IN BRISTOL, six kilometres east of the centre. Kingswood near Wotton-under-Edge lies twenty kilometres north at 51.63, -2.36. THE COUNTY COULD NOT HAVE DECIDED IT — both were Gloucestershire, the Bristol one until 1974 — and guessing from the name would have put this family's surname back in the Vale it came from rather than the city it moved to.

THE CHURCHYARD IS ALSO A FINDING IN ITSELF: 571 records and 402 headstone images, free and without an account. It is the first Bristol burial ground this archive can read end to end. Twentieth-century, so it answers nothing about the eighteenth — what it shows is the surname still standing in Bristol in 2008, four generations after Thomas Sinegar was married there by banns.

AND TOOK THE RECORD ATLAS SESSION'S CHALLENGE LITERALLY: does any probe here ask a different question from the one whose answer it records? Theirs had been a liveness check passing against a host that served nothing while 25 of 27 tests failed. Most of this archive's gates have been proved to fail in anger this fortnight — controls refused a `ctl` on a blocked row this week, atlas refused the Thornbury pin an hour ago, retired refused a restated reading, secrets refused a planted key, whosplit refused Miriam on its first run. THE ONE THAT HAS NEVER ANSWERED ANYTHING IS check_cites.py.

IT IS WIRED INTO NOTHING AND HAS NEVER RUN. It tests the links OUT of this site, which nothing else does, and a dead citation looks exactly like a live one on the page. I wired it into build.sh and took it straight back out, because the measurement said not to: 575 DISTINCT EXTERNAL URLS, one at a time, 12-SECOND TIMEOUT EACH, AND NO OUTPUT UNTIL THE LAST RETURNS. A run was stopped at eight minutes having printed nothing. And 428 OF THE 575 ARE MYHERITAGE LINKS carried in from the GEDCOM export rather than citations this archive chose — as written it would spend most of its time checking somebody else's footnotes. Work list 140, with what it needs to become usable. A step people disable is worse than no step.

AND THEN THE CORRECTION WAS WRONG TOO, WITHIN THE HOUR. It said SANIGER returns 25 burials and none in the United Kingdom. The same query at `size=50` returns FOUR IN ENGLAND: Andrew, Barbara and Dennis Sanigar all at HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, KINGSWOOD, and Maisie Sanigar at Scartho Road Cemetery, Grimsby. The «none» was the page size. Twentieth-century burials, so not evidence for the eighteenth-century questions — but three of this surname in one churchyard, and WHICH Kingswood is unresolved: there is one in Gloucestershire three miles from Wotton-under-Edge and another in Bristol.

THE SITE CANNOT BE SEARCHED BY URL AT ALL. `cemetery_country=United+Kingdom` is accepted and ignored — identical rows with and without it, French and American and Australian among them, which also means the SMITH «control» published an hour ago was never filtered. `page` is accepted and ignored: `page=7` returns the same first three records as `page=1`, and the footer reads «Page 1 of 200» whatever is asked. About ten thousand D'Arcy records exist and the first fifty are all a URL can reach. THE FOURTH SEARCH PARAMETER THIS ARCHIVE HAS FOUND ACCEPTED AND IGNORED, after FindMyPast's `place`, `sourcecategory`, and `yearofbirth` with `keywordsplace`. Usable for a positive, useless for a negative. [Own error 54](/corrections/).

AND A SOURCE THIS ARCHIVE HAD WRITTEN OFF IS OPEN. The Record Atlas session mentioned in passing that eight French departmental archives in its survey refuse a SCRIPTED request and open normally to a real browser, and suggested retesting anything written off that way. Four rows here carry «blocked». Two are account walls and genuinely shut. IRISHGENEALOGY.IE SURVIVED THE RETEST — still sitting on a Cloudflare interstitial after twenty-two seconds, not defeated and not going to be. AND BILLIONGRAVES WAS SIMPLY WRONG: it answers a browser at once, and the 403 and 400 behind the verdict were facts about the request.

WHAT IT HOLDS, NOW IT CAN BE ASKED: SANIGER returns 25 burials — United States, Canada, France, Australia — AND NONE IN THE UNITED KINGDOM. Control: SMITH filtered to the United Kingdom returns Swarkestone and Portslade in England and Forfar and Aberdeen in Scotland, so British cemeteries are in the index and this is a null rather than a gap. A weak null: the site is volunteer-photographed and thin in Britain, so it can support «not found here» and never «not buried». [Own error 53](/corrections/).

WENT BACK TO THE 24 PARENT LINKS LEFT UNDRAWN, and the first measurement of them had been against the wrong index. It counted «parent not in the tree» using ancestors.json, WHICH HOLDS ONLY DIRECT-LINE ANCESTORS — Joseph D'Arcy reads as «0 in tree» there while having a person page. Asked of the GEDCOM's 15,643 individuals instead, the picture changed, and seven more links were safe to draw.

JOSEPH D'ARCY'S SECOND FAMILY IS NOW DOCUMENTED ON THE CHARTS. Catherine Lucy Jane, John Hyde, Josephine, Frank Hyde and Joseph William were each baptised at Milford to «JOSEPH, Lt Col RA», and every one of their charts drew that father as «tree, untested». Charlotte D'Arcy's Chatham baptism of 1826 and Jane D'Arcy's christening at St Michael, Barbados in 1788 — the latter naming Robert D'Arcy as her father — are drawn too. 54 recorded relationships across 51 people, from 41 across 35 this morning. The mother of the Milford five is KATHERINE LUCY ELIZA in the register and is in the tree under no such spelling, so only the father is drawn: naming her would be guessing which of the tree's women she is.

AND A REFUSAL NOBODY HAD READ. The REL table carried «Charlotte Maria D'Arcy» pointing at George Pitt D'Arcy, and the tree calls her CHARLOTTE D'ARCY — so build_register.py had been printing «ambiguous or absent, so no edge was drawn» for her on every build, and the edge had simply never existed. It is drawn under the right name now and the dead entry is gone, because a refusal that fires every build and is never acted on is the «ok» line in a different costume.

AND THE SAME GAP WAS ON THE OTHER TWO TREE-DERIVED PAGES, so it was fixed as a class rather than a third time by hand. /graves omitted 26 documented burials and /households 8 documented census placements. The graves list includes JOHN SANIGER, HANNAH'S FATHER, BURIED AT BERKELEY ST MARY THE VIRGIN ON 16 JANUARY 1825, with Thomas Saniger of 1819 and Edward Saniger of Saniger, Gent., of 1739 beside him. /graves was never dishonest about it — it says «gathered from the tree» in its own first sentence — but saying where a list comes from is not the same as showing what it leaves out.

THE COMPUTATION LIVES IN ONE PLACE, site/src/lib/treegap.js, and /marriages was refactored onto it rather than left with its own copy. Three copies of one rule drift, and a surface quietly showing a different difference from its neighbour would be worse than the fault being fixed. All three now read «And N the tree does not carry» — 34, 26, 8 — computed each build, so documenting one more puts it on the page by itself.

THEN THE CHARTS. 30 of the 58 record lines that name a parent belonged to people whose pedigree drew no edge at all — documented parentage still rendering as «tree, untested». The cause is structural: REL is hand-kept and the record lines are generated, so a new record never becomes an edge unless somebody writes one. Six were added and drawn, taking the charts from 41 edges to 47 across 44 people. ONLY DISTINCTIVE FULL NAMES WERE USED: the automatic pass also offered «Mary», «Elizabeth» and «MARY» resolving to exactly one tree person each, and this family reuses forenames without mercy. Two of the eight proposed were refused as ambiguous by the tool itself and are named rather than drawn.

THEN THE ATLAS, WHICH CANNOT MAP ANY OF THE SEVEN PLACES THIS ARCHIVE HAS DOCUMENTED AND THE TREE DOES NOT HOLD. Four resolve to 52.531,-1.265, the geocode for the word ENGLAND, each stamped «exact»: Bourn (Catherine Georgiana West's burial), Lymington (Frank Hyde D'Arcy's marriage and Joseph D'Arcy's death district), Penzance (George Abbas died there), Milford (two D'Arcy baptisms). Two resolve to nothing: Bangor, where Robert West D'Arcy died, and Bombay, where he married.

AND THE SEVENTH IS THE ONE WORTH RECORDING. Thornbury looked like the single good case and was added to the map with Lydia Sanigar's death registration behind it. check_atlas.py REFUSED THE BUILD: Thornbury and Gloucestershire now shared 51.833,-2.167, and neither contains the other. It is the county centroid standing in for a market town twenty miles away. OWN ERROR 41 ATTEMPTED TWICE IN ONE HOUR, CAUGHT THE SECOND TIME BY THE GATE WRITTEN AFTER THE FIRST — and caught after I had already congratulated myself on avoiding it. The entry was removed; all seven are counted on the work list instead of guessed at.

THE TIMELINE IS HONEST AND WAS LEFT ALONE. Its dek says the point «is not when people were born — it is what was happening around them when they were», which is a stated curation rather than a claim of completeness, so a documented event missing from it is not a fault. /graves says «gathered from the tree» in its own first sentence. Those two needed nothing.

THEN THE SAME QUESTION OF THE DIAGRAMS, and /marriages was overclaiming. Its dek read «EVERY MARRIAGE THIS ARCHIVE CAN DATE, in order». The page is built from marriages.json, which build_family_pages.py derives from the GEDCOM — so what it actually showed was every marriage THE TREE can date. The difference is 34 marriages this archive holds a record for and the tree does not carry, AND ONE OF THEM IS HANNAH SANIGER'S OWN MARRIAGE TO JAMES WAKEFIELD AT BRISTOL ON 17 OCTOBER 1831, which is the founding marriage of the English line.

THE CLAIM IS CORRECTED AND THE DIFFERENCE IS NOW PUBLISHED. The page computes it at build time from person-records.json and dossiers.json against the couples table, so it cannot go stale: document a marriage and it appears there until the tree catches up. Among the 34 are William Sneyd and Mary Blackbourne at Madeley in 1769, Robert West D'Arcy at Bombay in 1846, Frank Hyde D'Arcy at Lymington in 1863, and the 1852 Bristol marriage of James Sanigar found a fortnight ago.

AND THE FIRST DRAFT OF THAT BLOCK MADE ITS OWN FALSE CLAIM: it said «the first of them is the founding marriage of the English line» while sorting the table alphabetically, which put Agnis Sainger at the top. Caught by reading the built page rather than the intention. /graves and /households were checked in the same pass and neither overclaims — graves says «gathered from the tree» in its own first sentence.
ASKED WHETHER THE RESEARCH REACHES THE PEOPLE AND NOT ONLY THE PAGES. Mostly yes, and four people were missed in two different ways.

THREE HAD NO RECORD LINE AT ALL, so neither surface could show them: CATHERINE SNEYD, who died aged four — death registered December quarter 1849, Stoke on Trent, GRO volume 17 page 114, with a national control returning exactly one such death in eight years; JAMES SANIGAR, whose 1852 Bristol marriage this archive found on 27 September; and LAURA SAYER, who is on the same page of the index and is almost certainly his wife. All three were written up, graded and published in prose, and none of them existed as a person anywhere on the site. The evidence gate reads register.json and checks that every line reaches its person — IT CANNOT SEE A PERSON WHO WAS NEVER GIVEN A LINE.

AND ONE WOMAN WAS SPLIT IN HALF. Joseph D'Arcy's first wife had two /who pages: «Lady Catherine Georgiana West» carried her two death notices, «Catherine Georgiana West» carried her burial and the Westminster baptisms of her sons. A reader landing on either saw half of her. The second line is this archive's own, added on 23 September under a name that already existed in another form.

A NEW GATE, AND IT FOUND A SECOND ONE ON ITS FIRST RUN. check_whosplit.py asks whether two dossiers differ only by a title or a trailing qualifier — «Lady X» beside «X», «X, née Y» beside «X» — which is the shape this archive actually produces. It immediately refused on MIRIAM WAKEFIELD, who is IN THE TREE and whose two most important records were parked on /who pages because the register filed them under her married forms: her sworn deposition, and her 1909 death registration NAMING HER MOTHER AS HANNAH SANIGER, which is the link into the Saniger line. Her person page carried four records and now carries six.

build_dossiers.py already guards against this and says so in its own comment — «duplicating them would split the same human in two» — but it compares the tree's names against the register's EXACTLY, so two different strings for one person never meet the test. The guard was real and the fault walked around it.

days.title: Two deaths looked for, neither found, and the reason is worth more than the search
found: /sanigers — the spelling table has been published since 21 September with no statement of what it counts
/bristol-chapels, /behind-the-paywall, /saniger-line — a target and two source lines, written and never rendered
/coverage — FreeBMD is transcribed unevenly by quarter AND by district, and says nothing when a quarter is missing
/searched — both of Joseph D'Arcy's elder sons' deaths, blocked by coverage rather than absent
did: CLEARED THE UNPUBLISHED BACKLOG, and the useful part is that «unpublished» turned out to be two different faults. Of eight passages the gate was reporting, TWO WERE THE CHECKER: sources.json carries literal <code> markup that was stripped from the page side and not the data side, and the coverage legend's glosses live in title= tooltips, which tag-stripping discarded. That is the THIRD normalisation fault in this one tool, after the markdown and the whitespace.

OF THE SIX THAT WERE REAL, FOUR WERE LOST AND TWO WERE DUPLICATES. The lost: /bristol-chapels never said what it was searching for, /behind-the-paywall and /saniger-line never named the record sets behind their findings, and /SANIGERS HAS CARRIED ITS SPELLING TABLE SINCE 21 SEPTEMBER WITH NO STATEMENT OF WHAT IT COUNTS — 27 spellings tried, 20 productive, 373 entries, one stated basis, and a floor rather than a total. All four published.

THE TWO DUPLICATES WERE REMOVED, NOT RENDERED, and the near-miss is the lesson. portsea.theFind held Joseph D'Arcy's 1780 baptism as seven structured fields, and the page's own opening already says all of it, including «the only document anywhere that names Major-General Robert D'Arcy as somebody's father» — which is the same claim as the field I was about to publish. Rendering it would have printed that record twice on one page. The reason for each removal is written into the file it was removed from.

WENT AFTER THE TWO SONS' DEATHS, because both died in Britain after civil registration and the GRO index is free through FreeBMD. Neither can be found there, and in both cases the quarter this archive needs is the one that is not transcribed.

GEORGE ABBAS KOOLI D'ARCY died on 22 October 1885, which registers in the December quarter. DARCY deaths for 1885 return March and June and stop. Control: SMITH deaths in the Penzance district across 1885 return March, June and September, each marked >99% transcribed, and NO DECEMBER. The gap is the quarter, not the surname.

ROBERT WEST D'ARCY died at Bangor on 14 June 1862. DARCY deaths for 1862 return March, September and December and no June — which alone could mean either no D'Arcy died that quarter or the quarter is missing. Control: SMITH deaths in the Bangor district across the WHOLE of 1862 return zero rows and not one quarter header, which cannot be a real result for a district that size. Bangor 1862 is simply not in the index.

SO NEITHER IS A NULL, and the coverage row now says why: FreeBMD prints its completeness beside a quarter it has — «(>99%)» — and prints NOTHING AT ALL for a quarter it does not, which is the one case that looks like evidence. Before quoting an absence from it, run a common surname at the same district and quarter.

A NOTE ON METHOD, because it nearly went wrong twice. The first run of the 1885 control was contaminated — a stray click had put SMITH into the spouse field as well, narrowing the result silently — and was re-run clean. And the search form's pixel coordinates could not be trusted: the screenshot frame changed height between calls, 505 then 600 then 500 against one viewport, so clicks computed from one frame missed in the next. The form was driven through its own controls instead, with every field read back before submitting.

found: three more tools chose a build directory by hardcoding it, including the one written for own error 49
eight gates accepted flags they did not take and ignored them. They refuse now
the deploy ran two of this archive's twelve gates. It runs twelve now
/sneyds — Catherine, dead at four, with her death registration and a national control
/worklist 139 — the unpublished backlog is 8, not the 57 published yesterday. Own error 50
did: AND FIXING THE EIGHT WAS NOT FIXING THE CLASS. The eight shared a symptom — a flag they swallowed — and the fix was scoped to the symptom. Asking the fuller question of every tool found three more that name a build directory by hardcoding `site/dist` and reading no environment at all: agree.py, which runs in every build here and has therefore been reporting on the shared dist of 23 SEPTEMBER, five days stale, 225 sources against the current build's 218 — and the seven are seven place pages this archive itself retired when it folded place-name variants, so the place-agreement report was checking agreement against places it had abolished; sitemap.py, which nothing references because the kit's is used; and CROSSREAD.PY, WHICH IS THE TOOL THIS ARCHIVE REPROACHED ITSELF THAT MORNING FOR NOT RUNNING — it would have graded the wrong build if it had been run. All three ask outdir now. [Own error 52](/corrections/).

AND THE FALSE FAILURE HAD A CAUSE IN THIS ARCHIVE'S CODE, not in the session that reported it. It ran `python3 tools/check_links.py --dist <a fresh build>` twice and got a FAIL both times. check_links.py has no argparse and takes no arguments, so `--dist` was SILENTLY SWALLOWED and the gate graded whatever stale dist was on disk while the fresh build sat untouched beside it. Two archives then held two different numbers for one question, and only asking for the exact command settled it.

EIGHT GATES WERE IN THAT POSITION — links, published, retired, controls, namefold, atlas, living-rule, secrets. A tool that ACCEPTS an argument and ignores it is worse than one that rejects it and worse than one that honours it, because the caller has no way to find out. They now refuse, name the directory they would have graded, and say that ARCHIVE_OUT is the way to point them at a build. Exit 2, verified.

TEN OF THIS ARCHIVE'S TWELVE GATES NEVER RAN ON THE DEPLOY. The landing session pointed out that check_links.py — the evidence gate, the one in the Mazza lineage — was wired into nothing. It was in build.sh, which runs on this machine; it was not in `npm run build`, which is what GitHub Actions runs, and Actions builds the site the public reads. Measured rather than accepted, and it was not one gate: atlas, controls, decisions, links, living-rule, namefold, published, retired, secrets and unpublished were all in that position. Only check_living.py had been wired. EVERY GATE WRITTEN YESTERDAY AND TODAY WAS AMONG THEM.

CI CANNOT SIMPLY RUN build.sh, because that begins by reading the GEDCOM and the GEDCOM is gitignored — it carries living people in full and Actions must never hold a copy. So the ten gates that need only committed data and built HTML are collected in tools/check_archive.py, wired into `npm run build`, and they now run on every deploy. The kit pin was not touched.

THE ARCHIVE'S OWN SENTENCE FROM THE DAY BEFORE APPLIES TO ITS TOOLS: only a page is a published claim, a file in the repository is not. A GATE NOTHING RUNS IS THE SAME THING — a check in the repository is not a check on the build.

A NEIGHBOURING SESSION SHARPENED YESTERDAY'S QUESTION and the sharper version found something. Not «does a finding reach a page» but «does it reach a page a reader would browse, or only a log page that points at itself». A record whose sole home is /searched is filed, not shown.

THE LOG PAGES ARE NOT A NEW LIST. retired.json already declares them — the pages permitted to restate a withdrawn reading BECAUSE THEIR SUBJECT IS THE WITHDRAWAL. The same set, declared for the same reason, so the two checks cannot drift apart.

IT FOUND CATHERINE SNEYD. Died at four; death registered December quarter 1849, Stoke on Trent, GRO volume 17 page 114; born Hanley 1845, mother's maiden name BIDDULPH; and a control across the whole of England and Wales for every Catherine Sneyd death between 1845 and 1852 returning EXACTLY ONE. sneyds.astro referred to none of it. She is on /sneyds now.

AND THE COUNT THAT FOUND HER WAS WRONG, for the second time in two days and in the same place. The comparison collapsed whitespace instead of removing it, so «ASHLEWORTH,» became «ASHLEWORTH ,» against a data side with no such space. 57 unpublished passages were really 8. The findings survived both bad counts and the counts did not, which is the lesson: a real absence survives a poor comparison and a false one does not. [Own error 50](/corrections/).

ONE CORRECTION OUTWARD TOO: the landing session flagged this archive as having no evidence gate. It has one, in check_links.py, and its docstring names the Mazza fault the estate's five other gates came from. It reads «189 record line(s) owed by register.json reach 61 of 61 people» on every build, and it is the gate that caught George Abbas Kooli D'Arcy yesterday.

did: ASKED WHETHER THE LAST FEW DAYS WERE ACTUALLY PUBLISHED, and checked the live site rather than the repository. Every commit clean, every deploy green, every page correct — and two things invisible anyway. THE ERRANDS PAGE NEVER RENDERED ITS OWN `why` FIELD: 46 of 66 rows carry a one-line statement of stakes, and the kit's component has no slot for it. And hannah-baptism.json held a block no template referred to — four tested claims about Hannah's mother including LYDIA SANIGAR'S DEATH REGISTRATION, September quarter 1851, Thornbury district, GRO volume 11 page 329, written on 16 September and published today. Neither was a research failure and neither was a build failure. A FILE IN THE REPOSITORY IS NOT A PUBLISHED CLAIM; ONLY A PAGE IS.

THE SWEEP THAT FOUND THEM IS NOW A TOOL, and its first run was wrong in the day's usual way. It stripped markdown from the data and not from the pages, and reported 201 unpublished passages where there were 71 — 130 of them the comparison rather than the archive. Both sides are folded identically now. 57 remain, reported on every build and never refused, because some prose in these files is deliberately internal and a check that cannot tell those apart gets turned off within a week.

THE TROVE KEY ARRIVED, ten days after the four questions were answered, and valid to December 2026. It was granted on four written undertakings, one of which is that NO ARTICLE FULL TEXT WOULD BE RETRIEVED — «the request is metadata only, newspaper and gazette titles, their place coverage and their date ranges». tools/trove.py calls the two titles endpoints and nothing else, and says in its own docstring that it must not be extended to article search: that would be a new conversation with the Library, not a quiet widening of a promise that was the reason the key was granted.

AND THE TABLE IS THE POINT. Question four of the Library's form asked why the API rather than the website, and the answer was that this archive publishes absences as well as findings. Here is what that buys: papers published AT the place, then anywhere in the colony — Parramatta 1849, 0 and 9; Brisbane 1856, 2 and 3; Brisbane 1902, 11 and 37; Brisbane 1936, 15 and 55. George Pitt D'Arcy died at Parramatta in 1849 and NO PARAMATTA PAPER OF THAT YEAR IS DIGITISED, but nine New South Wales papers are. In Brisbane in 1856 there are two in the whole colony, and an absence there is nearly worthless. Published openly at /trove-titles.json, as promised.

AND THEN ASKED WHAT IS ACTUALLY DIGITISED, title by title, for Queensland and New South Wales over 1826-1940 — 725 of 728, still inside the undertaking because an issue count per year is a date range. A TITLE'S RANGE IS NOT ITS HOLDINGS. Parramatta 1849: no paper published at Parramatta, but eight New South Wales papers hold the year and 675 issues survive, 312 of them THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD. AND THIS ARCHIVE ALREADY HOLDS HIS OBITUARY from one of them, found on the Trove website long before the key existed — which is own error 49, asserted in the same hour as a lecture to another archive about checking. What the holdings actually buy is the ability to state an absence across 675 issues and mean it. Brisbane 1856 is three papers and 154 issues. Brisbane 1902 is 36 of 37 in-range papers, 1936 is 54 of 55 — and those one-title gaps are the whole reason the question was worth asking.

A FOURTH ZERO THAT MEANT THE WRONG QUESTION. The holdings read 0 issues for every place and year, including Brisbane 1902 across 37 papers, which is impossible. JSON HAS NO INTEGER KEYS: the counts were written under int keys and come back under string ones, so every lookup missed. Caught by checking against a case that could not honestly be zero rather than by reading the output. That is four in one day — the gazette key, the flattened ranges, the state abbreviations, and this.

THREE PARSER FAULTS IN THE FIRST TEN MINUTES, all of the same family and all caught before anything was published. The gazette list comes back under the key `newspaper`, so asking for `gazette` returned 0 — one commit from publishing «Australia has no gazettes» as an open file; the endpoint's own total is now compared with what was parsed, and a disagreement refuses. The API's startDate and endDate FLATTEN a broken run, so «Clarion (Brisbane, Qld. : 1940 - 1943; 1945 - 1956)» read as covering 1944; 90 of the 2,052 titles have such a gap, and the ranges are kept apart now. And a title with no colon in its bracket put the date range into the place field, giving towns named 1933.

A CREDENTIAL IN A TRACKED FILE IS PUBLISHED ON THE NEXT PUSH AND CANNOT BE UNPUBLISHED. The key is in .env and .env is gitignored, but that is a fact about today's arrangement rather than a control. check_secrets.py reads what git actually TRACKS — not the working tree, or it would report .env every run until somebody turned it off — and refuses on anything credential-shaped. Verified by planting one and watching the build refuse.

THE SPINE WAS THE MOST CREDULOUS PAGE IN THE ARCHIVE ABOUT ITS OWN MOST CONTESTED CLAIM. /direct-line badged the six generations above the Hornby graft «Inferred»; their person pages badge them «Disputed» and /how-far-back calls the link unevidenced. The cause was a fallback: chip() returned the literal «unproven» for anyone the hand-kept table of seven does not carry, and the Evidence component folds that to «Inferred». Eight of fifteen badges on the page were that fallback. It now falls back to grade(), which computes the answer from provenance.json and is total — 7 Disputed, 6 Documented, 2 Family, and no invented grade. Found by applying a neighbouring session's correction to this archive's own code. [Own error 47](/corrections/).

AND WAS WRONG ABOUT THE PIN, IN A CORRECTION ISSUED TO SOMEBODY ELSE. This archive told the landing session that its pin was 2790d85 and not the 8ec58e6 they had read, and advised them to re-check all ten repositories. They did, from disk and from git HEAD, and they were right: fadb87c — a commit about gating a chart — had carried the pin to 8ec58e6 four commits back. The build prints the pin on every run and had printed 8ec58e6 three times. [Own error 48](/corrections/).

AND BUILT AN ANSWER TO IT, because naming a pattern is not fixing one. The landing session's reply to own error 48 was to report the DELTA rather than the state — speak only when the kit pin moves. The principle is right; the scope is the interesting part. Nearly every number in this build moves each run for good reasons, so a general delta report would be switched off within a week, which is the failure mode of every noisy check ever written. WHAT DOES NOT MOVE WITHOUT SOMEBODY DECIDING IT SHOULD IS A MUCH SMALLER SET: the kit pin, the living-person policy, the six named on purpose, the two rejected grafts with the counts /how-far-back publishes, and the pages exempt from the retired-reading gate. Five values, each an act of judgement. tools/check_decisions.py recomputes all five from their real sources and REFUSES if one has moved — not reports, refuses, because a decision changing is exactly where a deliberate act should be required, and editing decisions.json in the same commit is that act. Exercised in all four states: unchanged, moved, undeclared, and source unreadable, which is reported as unreadable rather than guessed at.

AND THE GATE WAS THEN TESTED IN THE TWO STATES IT HAD NOT BEEN. The landing session took it into the kit and sent back two corrections, both of which landed. FIRST: it compared decisions by SPELLING, so a declared list merely REORDERED — by a hand edit, by a merge, by any tool that rewrites JSON — was refused as a change. That is a false alarm, and a check that cries wolf gets turned off, which is the one way this gate fails completely. It compares canonically now. SECOND: the state «declared here and computed by nothing» had never been run, and when it was, it printed «is not declared» — the opposite of what had happened. A key with no probe reads exactly like a check and is not one; it now says so, and exits 1.

AND A SIXTH DECISION, from their account of a living woman another archive missed because its probe read the declaration while the gate read something else. This archive's living gate builds its allow-set from THREE lists in living.json — `named`, `namesakes` and `allow` — and only the six `named` were being watched. A phrase added to `namesakes` is exempted from the living rule just as effectively, and nothing here would have said so. The union is watched now: nine phrases, and adding one fails the build.

FOUND THE 1852 MARRIAGE BRISTOL ARCHIVES MENTIONED, free, in nine minutes. SANIGAR, JAMES — BRISTOL — 6A — 155 — DECEMBER QUARTER 1852, spelt the way they read the 1828 register and not the way this archive published it. Control first: SMITH in the same district and year returns 31, and every quarter is marked >99% transcribed.

AND A SURNAME FOR LAURA. The GRO prints everyone registered on a page, so Bristol 6a 155 carries four names — Sarah Godfrey, James Sanigar, LAURA SAYER, Henry Small. Lydia's baptism of 1866 names her mother Laura and gives no surname. IT IS AN INFERENCE, NOT A PAIRING THE INDEX STATES: the GRO does not pair spouses until 1912, and that is now a coverage row of its own.

THE CONTROL FAILED, AND THAT WAS THE FINDING. Asked whether the same instrument could find a marriage this archive already holds — Thomas Sinegar to Julia Marsh, 28 May 1871 — it returned nothing, in Bristol or in England. Asking for the bride instead returned Bristol 6a 131, and the man on that page is THOMAS LINEGAR. An S transcribed as an L.

WHICH PUTS A HOLE IN EVERY NULL ON THIS SURNAME. The wildcard is `S*N*G*` and the phonetic code is S526; both are blind at the first letter, and a record has now been found that neither can ever reach. The L side of 1852 has been checked and is empty. THE REST HAS NOT, AND THE NULLS ALREADY PUBLISHED ARE NULLS ABOUT THE S FORMS.

FREEBMD WAS NEVER BROKEN. This archive published it as «unusable — returns the results-page furniture with NO RESULT ROWS». Its Find control is an unlabelled image button; the only submits carrying text belong to the saved-search box, and pressing one returns a results-shaped page saying a saved-search file is missing. A week of this question went to FindMyPast instead, which showed eleven results and put every one behind an account. [Own error 46](/corrections/).

THE ESTATE CAME OUT OF ICLOUD. This repository lived in ~/Documents, which macOS syncs, and after an upgrade the sync re-materialised an older working tree on top of the current one: 59 paths dirty, files reporting as deleted and reappearing on disk a minute later, and nothing modified later than 24 September. Nothing was lost — every commit was already on origin — but for four days the tree on disk was not the tree that had been committed.
THE WORKING TREE WAS RECONCILED WITH HEAD and a full rebuild then regenerated every derived file byte-identical, except one.

THAT ONE WAS living.json, WHICH IS THE FILE THIS ARCHIVE PUBLISHES ABOUT THE LIVING-PERSON RULE. Its page count came back 849 where the build had made 854. The number was read from the shared `dist` of 23 September, not from the build just finished.

THE CAUSE WAS A DEFAULT MISTAKEN FOR A RULE. tools/outdir.py exists to make every gate grade the operator's build; check_living.py wired it in as an argparse default, and site/package.json passes `--dist dist` explicitly, so the default was never consulted. The gate checked 6 fewer pages and 14 fewer names for living-person leakage than the build contained, found none, and passed. Fixed by overriding after parsing, as the kit already did. [Own error 45](/corrections/).

THE TELL HAD BEEN ON SCREEN FOR FOUR DAYS. In the same run the kit's living gate said 858 pages and this archive's said 852. Two numbers for one build is the precise fault outdir.py was written to remove, and it is named in that module's own docstring. Both lines said ok, so neither was read.
THE CHECK NOW NAMES THE DIRECTORY IT READ whenever ARCHIVE_OUT is set, so a split verdict shows itself instead of waiting to be noticed in a tally nobody was adding up.

did: BRISTOL ARCHIVES READ THE 1828 MARRIAGE and answered every question the enquiry of 13 September asked. Free; the fee quoted for their research service is £13 for half an hour and none was charged.

THE ANSWER THAT MATTERS IS A NO. «Records from this time do not list fathers' names, nor abodes, ages, conditions or occupations.» Five of the seven things asked for are not absent from this entry — they are absent from every English marriage entry before 1837. That is a fact about the record class, not a null and not a blocked lookup, and it closes three errands instead of leaving them open forever.

AN ERRAND HAD BEEN CARRYING THE OPPOSITE BELIEF since the day it was written: «a Gloucestershire marriage entry names the father, as his son's did in 1871». The son's did because it is of 1871. /thomas-sinegar has printed both entries side by side, one with a father column and one without, since the day both were found.

THE REGISTER SPELLS IT SANIGAR, not SANIGRE. Both index sites read SANIGRE because both serve one FamilySearch transcription, so «confirmed on FindMyPast» was one reading seen twice. Neither spelling is asserted here now — the image is on Ancestry and nobody here has seen it.

WHAT THE ENTRY DID GIVE: by banns, and witnesses James Hall and Thomas Davey — with the archivist's own caveat that both «appear to witness multiple marriages in this church so are probably church officials», which empties the one answer that looked like a lead.

AND ONE RECORD NOBODY ASKED FOR: a marriage of 1852 for «what looks like Thomas's son, James», giving Thomas's occupation as Labourer. This archive does not hold it. It is after civil registration, so unlike his father's it names a father. Worklist 135.

did: FOUND THAT FINDMYPAST'S SURNAME BOX TAKES WILDCARDS, which is the whole of the day. `S*N*G*` over eleven years of one county returned a marriage this archive had published as not existing, and two spellings its own table did not hold.

COUNTED THE SPELLING TABLE PROPERLY. The five largest forms read row by row — 298 index entries are 246 baptisms. The repetition sits almost wholly in the two forms whose parishes were transcribed twice, so an entry count measures how often a parish was typed up as much as how often a name was written.

«NONE, IN ANY SPELLING» AT CHEW MAGNA WAS FALSE. Somerset Baptisms holds Charles Sinagar 1816 and William Sinegar 1822, children of SIMON and ELIZABETH — and a plain search for SINEGAR, one of the eight forms in use that day, returns the 1822 baptism on its own.

WHICH NAMES A GENERATION. Elizabeth Saniger, widow, 60, born Chew Magna, was already here living with her son William Saniger, 27, born Chew Magna, at Oxford Road in 1851. The register names her husband.

ERRAND 18 ANSWERED. The RG 4 Bristol chapel registers are transcribed on FindMyPast: `S*N*G*R` at Bristol returns nought against 133 Smith chapel baptisms there, and the surname's eight chapel entries are all at Dursley, Corn Meeting — so the family was Congregational, thirty miles up the scarp and not in Bristol.

LYDIA'S MARRIAGE ASKED WITHOUT A SPELLING LIST. 122 rows across Gloucestershire 1793-1803, every one read: six are this surname and not one is a John, not one marries a Lydia. The reading that it was hiding under an untried spelling is retired.

ENGLAND MARRIAGES 1538-1973 HOLDS NO HAMPSHIRE. Smith returns 0 there and 14,056 in Gloucestershire, which voided a null about Joseph D'Arcy's marriage. Re-asked of the county set, which holds this family's own 1779 wedding: 22 D'Arcy entries, no Joseph.
PORTSEA IS FINISHED. 44 D'Arcy baptisms in the county set and exactly one is Robert and Jean's, against a tree that gives them nine children.

THE NEWSPAPER ROUTE MEASURED AND CLOSED. FindMyPast's «Newspapers & Publications» is a name index to BMD notices, not the British Newspaper Archive: Robert D'Arcy returns 42 with nothing before 1857, Joseph 84 with nothing before 1914.

TWO GATES ADDED, each proved falsifiable by reintroducing the fault it catches: a FindMyPast null claiming «any spelling» must carry a wildcard, and a refused spelling fold must not reach the fold map.
AND BUILD.SH NOW SAYS WHETHER IT WAS KILLED OR REFUSED, after this session ran a `pkill` that matches every archive on the machine.

days.title: The last day of the subscription: the Hyde D'Arcys, and a claim withdrawn
did: NAMED JOSEPH D'ARCY'S FIVE CHILDREN, which this archive has wanted since it found his will. All five baptised at Milford to Joseph and KATHERINE LUCY ELIZA, the register calling him “Lt Col RA of MILFORD HOUSE” — an address nobody here had.
FRANK HYDE D'ARCY WAS BORN AT MADEIRA on 14 December 1838. Four words in a baptism note, and Joseph D'Arcy was on a Portuguese island in the Atlantic in the winter of 1838.
JOHN HYDE D'ARCY went to HARROW and died at Southampton on 28 June 1852, aged nineteen — reported as far as the Catholic Telegraph in Dublin.
FRANK HYDE D'ARCY died at Worcester on 15 June 1868, aged twenty-nine, five years after his Lymington wedding, and was brought home to be buried at Pennington.

And a grandson: FRANK HAMILTON HYDE D'ARCY, baptised at Croydon Common on 26 November 1868 — FIVE MONTHS AFTER HIS FATHER DIED — father entered as “Gentleman”, mother Anna Maria, of St James Road. He died at Chelmsford in 1910.
FOUND JEAN WARD'S DEATH NOTICE: Hampshire Chronicle, 24 March 1823 — “At Chatham, MRS. D'ARCY, THE WIFE OF MAJOR-GEN. D'ARCY, OF THE ROYAL ENGINEERS.”

WITHDREW A CLAIM MADE THE DAY BEFORE. /margaret-jones announced the 1843 notice as “the first record anywhere to give Robert D'Arcy a corps as well as a rank”. The 1823 notice does it twenty years earlier. Filed as an error, and the page now carries the correction above the claim.

FOUND THE 1806 MARRIAGE NOTICE: “At Chatham, CAPTAIN J. M. JONES, of the ROYAL DENBIGH MILITIA, to MISS D'ARCY, ELDEST DAUGHTER OF COL. D'ARCY, OF THE ROYAL ENGINEERS” — Oxford University and City Herald, 1 November 1806. The Chester Courant adds the church and the officiant.

Which disproved the correction made an hour earlier. The corps is on record in 1806, not 1823 and not 1843 — and the 1806 notice is the report of the very marriage the /margaret-jones page was built around. It also fixes Margaret as the ELDEST DAUGHTER.

DOCUMENTED JOSEPH D'ARCY'S PERSIAN DECORATION from the London Gazette of 30 June 1818: the Prince Regent's permission to wear the Second Class of the Imperial Order of the Lion and Sun, conferred by the King of Persia. Five papers carried it within the week. The page that said the archive “will not assert it from three letters after his name” now cites the grant.
CHASED THE TWO RICHARD D'ARCY DEATHS. Neither is the Richard of Priestlands — and one of them opened a family nobody here knew existed.

“At St Helier's, JERSEY, RICHARD, THIRD SON of the late LIEUT. COL. D'ARCY, ROYAL ARTILLERY, and LADY CATHERINE, SISTER OF THE PRESENT EARL DE LA WARR, aged 33” — Saint James's Chronicle, 23 May 1857.

And five years later: “CAPTAIN ROBERT D'ARCY, late of the INDIA COMPANY'S ARMY, son of the late COLONEL D'ARCY of the ROYAL ARTILLERY and LADY CATHERINE, DAUGHTER OF THE LATE AND SISTER OF THE PRESENT EARL DE LA WARR”, died at Bangor, 14 June 1862.

JOSEPH D'ARCY MARRIED THE DAUGHTER OF AN EARL. The tree has always given him a wife CATHERINE GEORGIANA WEST, married at Bath in November 1817, and this archive never looked at the name — WEST is the family name of the EARLS DE LA WARR. Two newspapers call her Lady Catherine independently.

So the five Milford children are his SECOND family. “Third son” means there was a first and a second: at least eight children across two marriages, where this morning the archive credited him with five.

Established a real null on the Priestlands Richard: only FIVE D'Arcy deaths were ever registered in the Lymington district — Joseph, his widow, and three moderns — and no Richard D'Arcy or ARCY is in the 1851 census anywhere in Britain.

OPENED FIND A GRAVE, a source this archive had never used, and found THREE D'Arcy memorials at CENTENARY MEMORIAL GARDENS, Brisbane: Kenneth Lindsay D'Arcy (1927–2010, plot Secret Garden), Audrey Dell D'Arcy (1929–2022, Garden of Reflection E/20) and CHRISTINE HILDA D'ARCY-EVANS (1930–2017, Garden of Reflection C/41), whose name this archive has never held.

And control-tested it first. Find a Grave's `locationId=state_2118` returns NO MATCHES for D'Arcy, Darcy, Sneyd — AND FOR SMITH, which is impossible, while Darcy worldwide returns 10,654. Searching within a named cemetery works; the location filter does not.

PUT FOUR MORE PLACES ON THE ATLAS by tidying what is handed to the geocoder — 153 placed became 157, and the approximates fell from 67 to 64. HTML escapes, “Som Eng” abbreviations and prose like “Christened in Berkeley” were stopping the lookup. What the page PRINTS is unchanged: the place as recorded.
Left thirteen unplaced rather than guess: Buckwall, Deinschwang, Neuhaus, Himley Hall, “Parish of Elmore” and “?” among them.
OPENED FOUR SOURCES THIS ARCHIVE HAD NEVER USED, and came away with one usable and three refusals — each with a reason and a control behind it.

ANTENATI holds 422 REGISTERS for ARIENZO at the Archivio di Stato di Caserta — Matrimoni processetti 63, Matrimoni 62, Nati 59, Morti 57, Diversi 45, from 1809 — digitised, free, and NOT NAME-INDEXED. A search for FALCO returns nothing; so does RUSSO, the commonest surname in Campania, which is the control that proves the index is missing rather than the family.

THE NLI CANNOT HELP THE LIMERICK LINE, and that is worth saying rather than searching. Its registers are CATHOLIC; Paul Cole Atkinson is recorded born at ST MARY'S, LIMERICK — the Church of Ireland cathedral parish — and Atkinson, Cole, Creech, Kent, Bowen and Peevers are Protestant settler names. The same shape as the Wicklow problem.

irishgenealogy.ie is behind a Cloudflare bot check for the THIRD time in this archive's life. RootsIreland is behind a subscription. SCOTLANDSPEOPLE answers ACCESS DENIED without an account, and no account was created and no credentials entered.
BILLIONGRAVES IS BLOCKED, NOT EMPTY: the page loads and its own search API answers 403 and 400, and the country list never finishes. Nothing was searched, so nothing is known — recorded that way.
Eight rows added to /coverage and three errands opened, so that the next pass starts from these verdicts instead of repeating them.

FOUND LADY CATHERINE'S BURIAL: CATHERINE GEORGIANA DARCY, AGED 36, “OF BATH”, buried 22 MARCH 1824 at BOURN, CAMBRIDGESHIRE. Born about 1788, twenty-nine at her Bath marriage, and dead six years before Joseph remarried — so the gap between his two families is now measured rather than assumed.

Her third son Richard was born about 1824, the year she died at thirty-six. Published as an inference and labelled as one; and why she is buried at Bourn, a hundred and fifty miles from Bath, is not explained.

FREEBMD OPENS WITHOUT A LOGIN AND RETURNS NOTHING. It accepts a POST and answers with the results-page furniture and no rows. Control: SMITH BIRTHS IN BRISTOL IN 1840 returns zero, which is impossible. Nothing was searched, and no null from it is recorded.

ROOTSCHAT REQUIRES AN ACCOUNT TO SEARCH, let alone to post. None was created. The two questions worth putting to it — the Holderness descent and the disproved Keele graft, both asked as “what would break this” — are drafted as errand 47.

GENEANET READS WITHOUT SIGNING IN, and no bot check appeared: 26 FALCO marriages at ARIENZO in Italy, Marriages 1809-1900, both parties named, including FALCO GIOVANNA married to CRISCI ANIELLO. Recorded as the Falco archive's ground rather than imported.

CLOSED THE BURIAL QUESTION. All three Sussex sisters are buried out of ST ANDREW'S OLD CHURCH, HOVE — and their entries are on THE SAME PAGE of the same register, TNA RG 37/65/2 page 47. CHARLOTTE 28 MAY 1869, JANE 10 JANUARY 1875, CATHERINE 23 JANUARY 1876.

Two exact dates where the archive held only GRO quarters — and Catherine's 23 January is the date the Horsham paper printed a fortnight after the event, so a parish register and a newspaper agree without either having seen the other.

FOUND ROBERT WEST D'ARCY, married at BOMBAY in 1846. The middle name is the find: WEST is Lady Catherine Georgiana's family name, so Joseph's son carried his mother's peerage surname to India. The transcript is paywalled even on a paid trial — indexed, not read.
And a third broken FindMyPast parameter: `sourcecategory` mangles to `life-events-bmds` and returns zero whatever else is asked. Any null drawn through it is worthless.

WILLIAM SNEYD OF MADELEY, the oldest name in the Sneyd line and until today a citation reading “Sneyd Web Site” with no death at all, now has TWO documented candidate burials at Madeley All Saints: 1819 aged 88, and 13 MAY 1827 AGED 84. The weaver married about April 1769 and fathered children to 1794, so the 1827 burial fits far better — and two candidates are two candidates, and the page says so.

CHARLOTTE CATHCART D'ARCY married ROBERT MEAD PEARSON at PARRAMATTA in 1859, registration 2618 — the town where her father died in 1849, and she would have been 34. A strong candidate for the Charlotte christened at Chatham eight days before the England sailed, and NOT an identification: the index spells the middle name two ways and the baptism gives none. Errand 48 is the certificate.
And recorded a seam left unworked as the trial expires: EIGHTY-ONE D'Arcy burials and memorials in Queensland Burials & Memorials, of which this archive holds one.

days.title: The Sussex sisters, documented
did: Took the three daughters added to this archive the same day out of its own family tree — Jane, Catherine and Charlotte — and tested them against the public record. All three hold.

Found all three CIVIL DEATH REGISTRATIONS, same district, seven years apart: Charlotte aged 73, Brighton Q2 1869, vol 2B p.152; Jane aged 87, Brighton Q1 1875, vol 2B p.203; Catherine aged 86, Brighton Q1 1876, vol 2B p.164.
The ages run back to births of about 1795, 1787 and 1789 against the tree's 1794, 1787 and 1789 — two exact, one a year out. These were web-tree claims yesterday.

Found Catherine's obituary: “On the 23rd ult., at BEDFORD SQUARE, BRIGHTON, MISS CATHARINE D'ARCY, aged 86” — Horsham, Petworth, Midhurst and Steyning Express, 8 February 1876. It confirms the exact date, confirms she never married, and gives an address.
Found that she left an estate: Index to Death Duty Registers, Court of Probate, Brighton 1876, TNA IR 27/396 — the likeliest document anywhere to name this family's English descendants after 1850.
Found all three sisters IN ONE HOUSEHOLD in the 1841 census — Western Buildings, Brighton, schedule 1912, with a servant, Sarah Harmer, 20.
Published the one thing that does not fit rather than burying it: the 1841 ages are 40, 39 and 35 when the sisters were 53, 51 and 46.

CAUGHT A SEARCH THAT LIES. A first pass reported no Jane D'Arcy of the right age in Sussex in 1871. The control — Jane Smith, same age, same county, same census — returned zero, which is impossible. Combining a year of birth with a place breaks FindMyPast's census query silently.
Re-ran the census work by year alone: the sisters are in none of 1851, 1861 or 1871 under any D*ARCY spelling. A real gap, now an errand rather than a false negative.
SEARCHED BY ADDRESS AND BY HOUSEHOLD INSTEAD OF BY NAME, and found all three sisters in the 1851 census at WESTERN COTTAGE, BRIGHTON — HO107/1646 f.357 p.59 sch.172.

THE CENSUS GIVES THEIR BIRTHPLACES: Jane and Catherine born BARBADOES, Charlotte born LYME, DORSET. An English government record confirming the West Indies posting that had rested on two Caribbean christenings and a family tree.
All three entered as LODGERS, UNMARRIED, occupation “FUND HOLDER” — living on invested capital, in rooms in somebody else's house.

Found why four days of searching had missed them: the surname is indexed as ARCY, the D' read as part of the forename. No D*ARCY query could reach them. They came out of a household search — Jane, with a Charlotte in the same house.
Searched 1861 four independent ways — surname, address, birthplace in Sussex, birthplace nationally — and they are in none of it.

READ THE 1851 CENSUS IMAGE rather than the transcript, and found two errors in the index. The enumerator writes “Jane D'Arcy” plainly — the apostrophe was read as the end of a forename, giving a surname of “Arcy”. And the address is “19 Western Cott” dittoed down to 22: the sisters are at 22 WESTERN COTTAGES, not at a house called Western Cottage.

Corrected a detail before publishing it: James Hayward, lodging house keeper, is schedule 173 on the next folio — the house NEXT DOOR, not the sisters' householder. Their own schedule holds three lodgers and no head.
Ran the 1861 census eight ways — surname, the right street, the widened street, Bedford Square, birthplace in Sussex, birthplace nationally, household fingerprint, and Falmer. They are in none of it.

days.title: Reading the archive against its own open questions
did: Wrote tools/crossread.py after yesterday's Constantine error: it holds the open questions as search terms, reads all 719 data files and built pages, and prints every place the terms appear except the page that owns the question.
Found that ROBERT AND JEAN HAD TEN CHILDREN on the family tree. This site's page about their family listed five. The Hornby page has said “ten children” in plain text for weeks.

Answered a question opened the previous day: JANE D'ARCY, born Barbados 15 December 1787, died at FALMER, SUSSEX in January 1875, AGED EIGHTY-EIGHT. Her tree birth date and her Barbados christening of March 1788 corroborate each other.
Added CATHERINE D'ARCY (1789–1876, born Barbados, died Brighton), two ANNA MARIAS who died small, and CHARLOTTE (1794–1869, born Lyme Regis, died Brighton) — four more children nobody here had named.
Bracketed the Barbados posting with no new record at all: children born Barbados in 1786, 1787 and 1789, then Portsmouth in 1792 and Lyme Regis in 1794. The Corps page had a twenty-four-year blank.

Found that the tree gives Robert D'Arcy a BROTHER — Constantine D'Arcy, born Barbados 1759, died Chatham 1778, appointed to De Lancey's Brigade on 1 June 1778 — which the Hornby page has never mentioned in all its argument about his parentage. Published with an explicit warning that it may be Robert's own son duplicated and back-dated.

Found that LYDIA has a birthplace (Wotton-under-Edge), two parents (William Jones and Sarah) and a death (7 July 1851, Berkeley) in this archive's data, none of which the page calling her unevidenced had mentioned. Her death is inside civil registration.
Same for CATHERINE COTTON, listed as an open question while the tree gives her birth, marriage, death and parents, all at Berkeley.

TESTED THE MARTHA WAKEFIELD CLAIM PROPERLY. The tree says she died at Maryborough, Queensland, on 23 April 1899, with a cemetery and a plot number, under the married name HURFORD. This site had searched for her in BRISTOL and concluded she “may never have existed”.

The free Queensland index has her: MARTHA HURFORD, died 23 April 1899, 1899/C/3288 — and names her parents as JOHN WAKEFIELD and a HUGHES. No Martha Wakefield dies in Queensland at all between 1855 and 1960. Another man's daughter had been grafted onto James and Hannah.

Filed two errors: searching the wrong country under the wrong surname, and repeating a false statement about this archive's own tree. And noted that the lesson had been filed once already, on 13 September, and not applied.

days.title: The last two days of the subscription, spent on wills, Barbados and a Canterbury newspaper
did: Established what FindMyPast can and cannot do for wills, before spending the trial on it. Its only Prerogative Court of Canterbury holdings are a wills index for 1750-1800 and an administrations index for 1660-1700 — NOTHING AFTER 1800. Robert D'Arcy's will of 1827, Joseph D'Arcy's of 1848 and John Maddock Jones's of 1844 are all beyond it. £3.50 each at Kew, and no free substitute.

Read the Gloucestershire probate index 1801-1858 for the Saniger line under wildcards rather than spellings — SAN*, SIN*, SYN*, SWA*. Two entries in 14,195: Abraham Synegar, cardmaker of Dursley (1813), and John Sanigar, carpenter of Oldbury-on-Severn (1822). NO SANIGER OF BERKELEY AT ALL. Control: 277 Smiths. Errand 7 closed.

Closed the Irish marriage-licence route for George Pitt D'Arcy and Maria White. The Diocesan and Prerogative Marriage Licence Bonds index holds 218,433 records, but sorted by year its DUBLIN entries effectively stop in 1741; Betham's abstracts end in 1810. Neither can hold an 1819 marriage. Six Maria Whites in the set, none marrying a D'Arcy; no George D'Arcy at all.
Searched the FindMyPast catalogue for consular and overseas registers and found NONE — the Le Havre deaths of 1843 are not reachable there. Filed as errand 35.
Chased Constantine D'Arcy, and found that this archive had been publishing half his story on one page while calling him unplaced on three others. FILED AS AN ERROR.

Found the record that settles him: the KENTISH GAZETTE of 14 May 1805 — “After a few weeks illness, the son of COL. D'ARCY, CHIEF ENGINEER OF CHATHAM LINES; his remains were interred with military honours.”
Which also gives Robert D'Arcy a post for the first time. Every other record of him gives a rank.

Cited both of Constantine's commissions to the London Gazette by issue and page, and found them printed in the Kentish Weekly Post of 12 June 1804 and in three papers of 29 March and 1 April 1805 — the last of which carries his father's lieutenant-colonelcy nine lines above his own first lieutenancy.
Counted Robert and Jean's children properly. There are six, not five: JANE D'ARCY, christened at St Michael, Barbados on 17 March 1788, has been in the register all along and on no family page.

Traced Joseph D'Arcy's line forward out of Priestlands. His son FRANK HYDE D'ARCY married ANNA MARIA SIMPSON at Lymington on 29 September 1863, announced in Thacker's Overland News for India and the Colonies. Fifty-two D'Arcy records at Lymington, running to an electoral roll of 2021 — a living English branch.
Found a second Kew document for Joseph's estate: the Index to Death Duty Registers gives him at IR 27/284, which leads to a register naming legatees and executors.
